PCA projection.
For each inspected layer and denoising step, we collect the target frame’s block-output features and project the spatial tokens onto three principal components. PCA is fitted independently for each layer–step pair, with a fixed random seed and deterministic component signs. Each projected channel is scaled using its first and 99th percentiles for RGB display. Because each projection is fitted independently, we compare the spatial organization of regions within each visualization rather than matching colors across cells. As discussed in
Section
3.1
, these maps reveal where recognizable scene structure emerges across noise levels and network depth: little coherent structure is visible in the noise-dominated region, scene regions begin to take shape in the structure-formation region, and the scene layout becomes more clearly defined in the structure-established region. The onset of recognizable structure occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and in shallower layers at lower noise. Viewed alongside the attention maps, the PCA features help distinguish the emergence of scene structure from the development of cross-frame associations, showing that attention can still favor competing regions even when the scene layout is recognizable. This joint analysis motivates placing correspondence supervision near the structure-formation stage and adapting the supervised layer to the noise timestep.
Attention readout.
At the same layer and step, we extract queries and keys after normalization and rotary positional encoding. For the fixed source query, each head’s dot-product scores are softmax-normalized over all video keys. We then retain the target-frame slice and average the resulting probabilities over heads. This readout differs from both the block-output features used for PCA and the learned aggregation MLP used during training. Target-frame responses are displayed after normalization by each map’s maximum, with color mapping and interpolation used only for visualization. Thus, the color scale indicates relative spatial response within a map, not an absolute probability shared across layers or noise levels.
The denoising axis uses the actual model noise timesteps along the sampled inference trajectory. The noise-dependent shift in structure formation motivates our layer-routing schedule, whose generation performance is evaluated against fixed-layer and alternative schedules in
Table
6
.

Heatmaps are normalized within each target frame and displayed with contrast adjustment to highlight the spatial concentration of attention responses. The examples illustrate that selected heads can associate observations of static surfaces and moving object parts.
Appendix F
Limitations and Future Work
GAD
improves scene and dynamic consistency across all three video backbones by transferring geometric correspondences during training, while preserving the original inference procedure. Its current design suggests three directions for further improvement.
More reliable correspondence targets.
Our results demonstrate that attention distillation with geometric correspondence targets improves video consistency. The current implementation extracts these targets from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention, making their quality dependent on the teacher’s matching ability and spatial resolution. This raises a natural question: can more reliable correspondences further improve the effectiveness of attention distillation? Stronger correspondence estimators or complementary sources of matching evidence could provide more accurate and complete supervision, particularly for ambiguous appearance, occlusion, and moving objects. The correspondence-based formulation of
GAD
provides a basis for exploring such alternatives to the current geometry teacher.
Adaptive supervision placement.
Our noise-timestep routing improves geometric metrics over fixed-layer supervision, demonstrating the value of adapting supervision depth to the denoising state. The current layer assignment depends only on the noise timestep and remains fixed throughout training. As the video model learns, the layers that benefit most from correspondence supervision may also change. Conditioning routing jointly on noise timestep and training progress could better match supervision to the model’s evolving representations, extending the current mechanism while preserving the original inference procedure.
Extension to autoregressive video generation.
GAD
improves static and dynamic consistency in Wan’s bidirectional video models. Autoregressive video generation offers a natural next setting, where preserving scene identity over long rollouts and maintaining coherent object motion remain important challenges. The principle of guiding attention with correspondences also applies to associations between newly generated content and preceding frames. Adapting the distillation objectives to the available temporal context under causal attention could help autoregressive models retain scene structure and moving-object identity as generation proceeds. This offers a promising route to extending the benefits demonstrated here to autoregressive generation.

article.headline: 把几何模型的注意力蒸馏进视频扩散模型
article.lede: 冻结的几何模型提供跨帧对应关系，训练时用来监督视频注意力，推理阶段不增加任何开销。
article.problem: 视频扩散模型能生成视觉上可信的短片，却难以在视角变化和物体运动下保持场景几何与物体结构。作者进一步发现，视频模型的跨帧注意力本身就无法可靠地定位同一场景元素，响应往往散落在多个区域，即使场景结构已经清晰浮现。
article.method: GAD 从冻结的几何基础模型 VGGT-Ω（1B）的注意力中提取跨帧对应点，只对干净视频做一次前向并缓存，把目标帧获得的总注意力质量作为可靠性权重，对可能不可靠的匹配降权。训练时在视频 DiT 的某一层上，用高斯平滑后的软目标做配对监督（帧对内的空间判别）和轨迹监督（同一源点对多帧的时间覆盖），并与原 flow-matching 损失联合优化。由于结构形成在高噪声时出现在深层、低噪声时出现在浅层，监督层按噪声时间步路由（t<850 用 L5，850≤t<950 用 L15，t≥950 用 L25）。
article.results: 在三个 Wan 骨干上，GAD 在 RealEstate10K、DL3DV-10K 的 15 秒长视频生成和 OmniWorld-Game 的 5 秒动态生成中均优于对应基线。Wan2.2 5B 上跨帧匹配命中率相对提升至少 30%：RealEstate10K 从 0.263 升到 0.350，DL3DV-10K 从 0.257 升到 0.335，旋转误差从 9.573 降到 4.890 度。Wan2.1 14B 在两个数据集的全部七项指标上取得最优。动态集上 Wan2.2 5B 的主体一致性从 0.825 升到 0.853、背景一致性从 0.900 升到 0.913。消融显示，噪声路由（R8）优于所有固定层方案（如 L25 全噪声 6.540 度）；而不用置信度加权时，命中率反而低于 Wan 基线（0.230 对 0.257）。推理时间与峰值显存基本不变。
article.why_it_matters: 监督只发生在训练阶段，推理时不需要教师模型、对应缓存或额外模块，这使它可以直接叠加到现有视频 DiT 上，为交互式世界建模、机器人规划和自动驾驶仿真提供更长期一致的视频生成。
article.limitations: 对应目标的质量受限于 VGGT-Ω 1B 教师的匹配能力和空间分辨率，遮挡、运动物体与外观歧义处仍是短板；层路由只在训练前按噪声时间步固定，不随模型表示演化调整，且仅在双向 Wan 模型上验证，自回归生成未测试。另外 5 秒与 10 秒设置下 FID/FVD 有小幅退步（5 秒 FID 从 26.85 升到 27.63）。
article.figure_caption_zh: 冻结的几何教师从干净视频中提取对应关系，在去噪过程中引导视频模型的注意力，该监督只在训练时加入，不改变推理流程。

figure.caption: {Overview of .} Correspondences extracted by a frozen geometry teacher from clean videos guide the video model's attention during denoising. The correspondence supervision complements the generation objective during training, without changing the inference procedure.

page_papers.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
page_papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
page_papers.content:
Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
Woobin Park
Jaeyeon Kim
Yilun Du
Sitan Chen
Bohyung Han
Affiliation:
Seoul National University
Affiliation:
Harvard University
⋆
Equal contribution
Summer 2026
Abstract
Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference.
This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce
Priming Models
, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a
fixed
noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training.
Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training.
Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at
256
×
256
256\times 256
resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of
1.19
1.19
among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at
https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming
.
Figure 1:
Priming Models
dramatically improve the training compute vs. FID trade-off on ImageNet (
left
). Simple reconstruction pretraining provides an effective initialization that makes subsequent distributional post-training substantially more efficient (
right
).
1
Introduction
A central goal of generative modeling is to achieve high sample quality with efficient training and inference. Diffusion and flow-based models
(
Song et al., 2020
;
Ho et al., 2020
;
Lipman et al., 2022
;
Albergo et al., 2025
)
have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities and now serve as backbones for several domains
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Abramson et al., 2024
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
, but they rely on iterative sampling with multiple network evaluations.
This has motivated considerable effort toward one- and few-step generation
(
Salimans and Ho, 2022
)
. Much of this progress builds on diffusion and flow formulations, including consistency-based modeling
(
Song et al., 2023
;
Lu and Song, 2025
)
, flow-map learning
(
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Geng et al., 2026b
)
, and distributional distillation
(
Luo et al., 2023
;
Yin et al., 2024a
;
Yin et al., 2024b
)
. While promising, these approaches require a considerable amount of extra machinery to work, like specialized stabilization strategies, Jacobian–vector products, classifier-free guidance, a teacher to distill from, etc.
A complementary approach is to train a generator by directly matching its output distribution to the data distribution. This naturally supports generation in a single network evaluation and has a long history in GANs
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
)
and maximum mean discrepancy-based generators
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
)
. Translating these objectives into effective training, however, requires significant engineering effort
(
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
.
This latter approach has seen a recent resurgence of interest, with Drifting Models
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
and W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
demonstrating that direct distributional learning can produce high-quality one-step generators at scale. Their training recipes nevertheless rely on longer training-time schedules and subtle tricks like style-conditioning
(
Karras et al., 2019
)
. Thus, the simplicity of one-step inference still comes at the cost of substantial complexity in getting these models to train.
In this work, we therefore ask:
Does training a one-step generator need to be this complicated?
We introduce
Priming Models
, a drastically more straightforward framework for one-step generative modeling with just two basic components:
[Stage 1] Reconstruction pretraining:
We pretrain the network with a simple reconstruction objective – in fact, even denoising at a
fixed
corruption level suffices.
[Stage 2] Distributional post-training:
We use the pretrained network directly as a one-step
generator that maps Gaussian noise to samples, then
refine it by matching generated and real distributions
in feature space, e.g., using an optimal transport loss.
Empirically,
Priming Models
achieve strong performance with substantially reduced training compute across three visual domains:
•
ImageNet
: Priming Models achieve state-of-the-art FID (
1.19
)
1
1
1
FD-loss
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
reports FID 0.72 for pixel MeanFlow by directly optimizing Fréchet Distance. We exclude this configuration from comparison and revisit this in Section
4.2
.
and Fréchet distances across other feature spaces among one-step generators, outperforming Pixel MeanFlow
(
Lu et al., 2026b
)
, Drifting
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
, and even multistep diffusion baseline JiT
(
Li and He, 2026
)
, with approximately
10
×
10\times
less compute than Drifting (Figure
1
, left).
•
Text-to-Image
: Priming Models substantially outperform one-step MeanFlow on GenEval and DPG, while reducing training compute by a factor of
1.9
.
•
World models
: Priming Models outperform the Drifting baseline
(
Lu et al., 2026a
)
with approximately half the training compute, while also achieving performance comparable to the (multi-step) flow matching baseline.
A key factor behind our strong empirical results is that
reconstruction pretraining substantially accelerates distributional post-training
(Figure
1
, right). Without the former, even when the distributional objective provides useful correction directions, the network’s Jacobian may hinder how effectively the parameters update to realize these improvements. Through controlled experiments, we demonstrate that reconstruction pretraining ameliorates this by aligning the Jacobian and shaping how readily the model’s outputs can be refined.
Together, our findings suggest a surprisingly minimal design principle for generative modeling: use reconstruction pretraining to
prepare
a generator for distributional post-training. Priming Models realize this principle, enabling high-quality one-step generators to be efficiently trained from scratch.
Figure 2:
One-step samples from Priming Models across three visual domains.
2
Priming Models
We first present our motivation behind
Priming Models
. Distributional objectives, such as Sinkhorn divergence or Wasserstein distance, offer a natural approach to one-step generative modeling by directly matching generated and real distributions. The central challenge, however, lies in translating these objectives into effective training procedures, a difficulty that helped motivate interest in alternatives such as diffusion models
(
Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021
)
. Indeed, early maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)-based generators were demonstrated on relatively small datasets
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
;
Genevay et al., 2018
)
, while GANs have achieved high-quality generation at scale
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
;
Arjovsky et al., 2017
;
Brock et al., 2018
;
Karras et al., 2019
;
Sauer et al., 2022
)
but remain sensitive to optimization
(
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
.
(a) Drifting-L
(b) W-Flow XL/2

More recently, Drifting Models
(
Deng et al., 2026

and W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026

1,280

We find that fixing these style embeddings yields only marginal differences between images
across different Gaussian noises
(Figure

Taken together, these observations suggest that optimizing distributional objectives from scratch, especially without these tweaks, remains challenging. This leads us to ask:
Question:
Can a suitable initialization make distributional post-training more effective?
Our intuition is that distributional training is challenging from scratch because at the start, the network has no information about the structure of natural images. To that end, we seek to first learn a related capability: recovering clean-image structure from corrupted inputs. Denoising reconstruction provides a natural way to learn this capability. Corrupted inputs retain information about the underlying images to guide recovery, while their clean counterparts provide direct supervision.
Our hypothesis is that learning to reconstruct provides a useful initialization for subsequent distributional optimization. This motivates
reconstruction pretraining
as a
first stage
toward learning the full noise-to-image mapping.

Comparison with other prior work.
Mainstream approaches to one-step generation build on diffusion or flow-matching trajectories
(
Liu et al., 2023a
;
Song et al., 2023
;
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Salimans and Ho, 2022
;
Yin et al., 2024b
)
. In contrast, Priming Models require neither prescribed trajectories nor a pretrained diffusion or flow model.
Recent work
(
Feng et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
uses distributional losses to improve already strong one-step generators. In Priming Models, reconstruction pretraining produces poor initial one-step samples (Figure
1
, right), and distributional post-training enables high-quality generation.
As noted at the beginning of Section
2
, Drifting
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
and W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
train models from scratch using distributional losses. Priming is more efficient than these methods and does not rely on additional modeling components such as classifier-free guidance or style embeddings; refer to Section
3
.
Most closely related to our work, D2O
(
Zheng and Yang, 2025
)
and
Yang et al. (2026, Section 4.3)
demonstrate the conversion of multi-step diffusion models into one-step generators. Priming Models build on this perspective, but our results show that starting from a multi-step model is unnecessary: even denoising at a single fixed noise level without time conditioning, as well as alternative pretraining objectives (Section
4.1
), can provide an effective initialization for distributional post-training. Appendix
A
provides further discussion.

Fréchet distance
(
Dowson and Landau, 1982
)
is widely used to evaluate generative models, but directly optimizing it was believed to be challenging, as reliable estimation typically requires tens of thousands of samples. FD-loss
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
addresses this challenge by accumulating feature statistics across training steps through a feature queue or exponential moving averages, while backpropagating only through the current batch, and has demonstrated consistent improvements in pretrained one-step generators.
We show that FD-loss also fits within the Priming Model framework as an alternative distributional post-training objective. Applied to the pretrained Priming-B checkpoint, it yields efficient post-training; we provide the setup and results in Appendix

5
Conclusion
In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generative models end-to-end. Reconstruction pretraining prepares the generator for efficient distributional post-training, enabling strong empirical performance across multiple visual domains.
That said, our work leaves several open questions. Priming Models rely on pretrained feature encoders. Although we demonstrate our method with multiple sets of feature encoders, this dependence raises the question of whether it can be eliminated. The relationship between reconstruction pretraining and Jacobian alignment also warrants deeper investigation. Finally, closing the remaining performance gap with multi-step diffusion and flow models remains an important challenge.
Outlook.
More broadly, our results suggest that we may be overthinking the problem: the specialized formulations and elaborate training machinery used in prior work are not the only path to train one-step generators. We hope our work opens the door to simpler and more scalable approaches to one-step generative modeling.

Appendix A
Related Work
In this section, we review prior work on one- and few-step generative modeling, organized by their methodological category.
Category 1: Trajectory straightening and flow-map learning.
These lines of work obtain few-step generative models by learning from a diffusion or probability-flow trajectory. Progressive distillation repeatedly compresses a teacher sampler into fewer steps
(
Salimans and Ho, 2022
)
. Consistency Models instead enforce agreement among predictions made at different points along the same trajectory
(
Song et al., 2023
)
, while subsequent work improves their stability and scaling or extends consistency to trajectory segments
(
Geng et al., 2025
;
Song and Dhariwal, 2024
;
Lu and Song, 2025
;
Kim et al., 2024
)
. Rectified Flow and reflow
(
Liu et al., 2023a
;
Liu et al., 2023b
)
seek straighter transport paths that are easier to integrate in few steps. These straightening methods modify the coupling and resulting trajectory so that coarse numerical integration can accurately reach its endpoint.
A related but distinct family learns the finite-time transition across an interval of a flow-matching trajectory, such as a flow map or average velocity. This includes Flow Map Matching, Shortcut Models, MeanFlow, Improved MeanFlow, and Inductive Moment Matching
(
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Frans et al., 2025
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Geng et al., 2026b
;
Zhou et al., 2025
)
. These methods differ in their targets and training estimators, but generally supervise a particular time-dependent transport or consistency relation.
Priming:
Priming Models do not attempt to recover a prescribed trajectory or flow map: reconstruction pretraining provides an initialization for the network, which we then directly use as a one-step generator.
Category 2: Teacher-guided distillation.
Another line of work distills a pretrained diffusion teacher into a one-step student, with much of the focus on designing effective distillation objectives. Diff-Instruct
(
Luo et al., 2023
)
uses score-based distributional objectives derived from a diffusion teacher, while DMD and DMD2
(
Yin et al., 2024b
;
Yin et al., 2024a
)
optimize the student using the difference between teacher and student score estimates. Score Identity Distillation
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
provides a related score-based formulation. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation combines score distillation with an adversarial objective to improve fidelity in the low-step regime
(
Sauer et al., 2024
)
.
Priming:
These approaches inherit the cost and machinery required to obtain and query that teacher. In contrast, Priming Models are trained from scratch and therefore do not require a pretrained teacher.
Category 3:Distributional loss (from scratch).
Directly matching a generator distribution to the data distribution has a long history. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) learn a one-pass generator through an adversarially trained discriminator
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
)
, with Wasserstein objectives and regularization improving the geometry and stability of training
(
Arjovsky et al., 2017
;
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
. Generative Moment Matching Networks use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in place of adversarial discrimination, while MMD-GANs further learn the MMD kernel adversarially
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
)
.
Genevay et al. (2018)
trains implicit generative models directly using a Sinkhorn divergence. These works, however, are limited in empirical scope and, more importantly, differ from Priming Models in that we apply the distributional objective after a reconstruction pretraining stage.
Recent works revisit direct one-step learning at a more practical scale. YOSO
(
Luo et al., 2024
)
stabilizes adversarial one-step training through a self-cooperative diffusion GAN, while Adversarial Flow
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
trains with an adversarial objective but constrains the generator to learn the deterministic transport map associated with flow matching.
Priming:
Priming Models share the goal of direct distribution matching, but do not optimize it from random initialization: reconstruction pretraining first teaches the generator to correct corrupted inputs toward clean images, after which a distributional objective refines it into a one-step generator.
Category 3-1: Drifting Models.
Drifting Models
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
construct an attraction-repulsion field using a normalized Laplacian kernel and train the generator to match stop-gradient targets obtained by displacing its generated features along this field. W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
derives a training-time velocity field from the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Sinkhorn divergence, using barycentric projections computed from entropic optimal transport plans.
Van Assel et al. (2026)
additionally examine how the choice of frozen feature space affects transport stability in distribution matching.
Priming:
Priming Models introduce reconstruction pretraining before distributional optimization, and this stage is key to our strong compute vs. quality trade-off.
Our implementation also seeks to dispense with the additional engineering machinery used in these works. Both reported ImageNet architectures include learned random style embeddings, and both frameworks support classifier-free guidance; Drifting additionally normalizes its constructed drift field. Priming does not use these additional mechanisms and instead optimizes an OT-based distributional surrogate. All four models reported in Section
3
share exactly the same post-training configuration, further illustrating the simplicity of our approach.
This suggests that reconstruction pretraining can make distributional optimization more efficient while supporting a simpler training recipe. We hypothesize that this initialization reduces the need for additional training mechanisms, although our experiments do not isolate their individual contributions.
Category 4: Distributional loss (fine-tuning).
Distributional objectives have also been used to adapt pretrained generative models. MMD-DDM
(
Aiello et al., 2023
)
fine-tunes pretrained diffusion models with MMD to improve quality under a restricted sampling-step budget. DiffRatio
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
estimates the density ratio between noisy real and generated distributions to train a one-step model without a teacher score. FD-loss
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
makes feature-space Fréchet distance practical as a training objective by maintaining population-level feature statistics, and applies it to pretrained one- and multi-step generators. More recently, iRDM
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
scales MMD-based post-training across multiple pretrained representation spaces.
Most closely related to our work, D2O
(
Zheng and Yang, 2025
)
shows that adversarial fine-tuning alone can convert a pretrained diffusion model into a one-step generator, while
Yang et al. (2026, Section 4.3)
show that FD-loss can convert JiT, a multi-step diffusion model, into a competitive one-step generator.
Priming:
Priming Models build on the perspective that pretraining can prepare a network for subsequent distributional optimization. We investigate how simple this pretraining task can be, showing that reconstruction—even denoising at a single fixed noise level without noise-level conditioning—can provide an effective initialization for our distributional training, despite poor initial one-step samples (Figure
1
, right). We further examine alternative pretraining tasks (Section
4.1
) within the same framework.
Finally, viewing reconstruction pretraining and distributional post-training as a complete training procedure also enables comparisons with prior methods based on total training compute across both stages, measured in EFLOPs.

article.headline: 两阶段预训练让一步生成训练算力降一个量级
article.lede: 先用固定噪声水平的去噪重建做预训练，再做特征空间分布微调，Priming Models 在 ImageNet 一步生成上
article.problem: 扩散与流匹配模型推理时需多次网络评估，一步生成成为研究热点，但现有方法依赖一致性建模、流映射、蒸馏教师、无分类器引导、风格嵌入等复杂训练机制。直接从零优化分布匹配目标（如 Sinkhorn、MMD）又长期受困于优化不稳定，需要大量工程技巧。论文因此追问：训练一步生成器真的需要这么复杂吗？
article.method: 作者提出 Priming Models 两阶段框架：第一阶段用重建目标预训练同一网络，最简单的实例是固定噪声水平 s=0.8 的像素去噪，并可选加 LPIPS 与 ConvNeXt 感知损失；第二阶段直接把该网络当作从高斯噪声到样本的一步生成器，在冻结特征空间（ResNet-MAE、ConvNeXt 等）中用带 stop-gradient 的 Sinkhorn/OT 代理损失匹配生成分布与真实分布。作者还用受控实验测量损失梯度子空间上的归一化 Jacobian 响应，论证重建预训练通过改善 Jacobian 对齐来加速分布后训练。
article.results: ImageNet 256×256 上，Priming-L（160 epoch 预训练）取得 FID 1.19 与 FDr5 7.10，为表中所列一步生成器最优，总训练算力 238.95 EFLOPs；论文称相比 Drifting 约少用 10 倍算力，且 FID 优于 Pixel MeanFlow、Drifting 与多步基线 JiT-H。文本到图像方面，logit-normal 预训练变体一步生成取得 GenEval 0.818、DPG-Bench 82.16，优于一步 MeanFlow（0.548 / 76.49）；固定 s=0.8 的版本为 0.740 / 81.30，总算力 293.53 EFLOPs，相对 MeanFlow 基线减少 1.86 倍。世界模型上，RT-1 训练算力 12.37 EFLOPs，比 DriftWorld 的 30.71 少 59.7%；Bridge-V2 为 9.50 对 37.05，少 74.4%，且除 RT-1 的 FVD 外所有质量指标均优。
article.why_it_matters: 它把一步生成的门槛从复杂专用机制拉回到「重建预训练 + 分布后训练」两个基本组件，并用 EFLOPs 统一核算两阶段总训练成本，为一步生成的可扩展训练提供了一个极简基线。
article.limitations: 方法依赖冻结的预训练特征编码器，作者自己也把「能否去掉这一依赖」列为开放问题；与多步扩散/流模型相比仍有性能差距，RT-1 上 FVD 30.96 也略逊于 32 步 flow matching 的 27.24。此外论文脚注提到 FD-loss 报告的直接优化 Fréchet 距离的 FID 0.72 被排除在比较之外，而用 SigLIP/MAE/Inception 做后训练特征时 FDr5 的改善并非独立留出特征结果。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图 1：Priming Models 显著改善 ImageNet 上训练算力与 FID 的权衡（左），简单的重建预训练提供了有效初始化，使后续分布后训练大幅提效（右）。

page_papers.title: Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
page_papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.

Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
Zhiyuan Zhou
Sergey Levine
Affiliation:
UC Berkeley
Abstract
Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naïvely training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method,
Advantage Guidance
, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model’s ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.

1
Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of improving policy performance beyond what is shown in the data, and can in theory outperform imitation learning under suitable conditions
[
46
,
30
]
.
However, RL algorithms suffer from lots of instability and hyperparameter sensitivity issues in practice
[
49
,
17
,
22
]
, especially over off-policy or offline data.
Imitation learning, on the other hand, has been shown to be stable and scalable for policy training with modern generative modeling techniques like diffusion and flow matching.
This raises the question:
can we perform policy training with something as simple and stable as imitation learning, but as performant as RL?
To achieve the stability of imitation learning, one might be tempted to directly apply the supervised-learning loss function, training the policy to maximize the likelihood of actions seen in the data.
Previous works have explored accomplishing this with conditional, filtered, or weighted supervised learning
[
13
]
.
One set of methods, which we will refer to as
advantage-conditioned methods
[
28
,
2
,
18
,
42
]
, resorts to training a policy conditioned on advantage values, which estimate how “good” actions are.
During inference, the policy is queried with a high advantage to generate “good” actions.
Unfortunately, such naïve advantage-conditioned policies typically underperform dedicated RL methods (see
Figure
1
).
This is in part because advantage-conditioning does not generally result in a policy that always favors actions with higher advantages as RL policies do: the resulting policy is restricted to the queried advantage level, and this restricts the degree of policy improvement.
Moreover, we find it difficult to train a policy to respond to advantage conditioning in the first place: the policy often cannot match the requested advantage (see
Figure
1
), and can ignore the conditioning altogether and revert to unconditional imitation.
In this work, our goal is to train a policy with the simple and stable supervised learning objective conditional on continuous advantage estimates, while enabling the policy to generate actions that maximize advantage.
To accomplish this, we first derive a diffusion guidance formulation we call
contrastive guidance
for sampling at test time, which can target actions that maximize the advantage under a KL behavior constraint.
Then, to effectively train a flow-matching conditional policy that responds to the conditional values, we re-parameterize the conditional policy as a residual flow on top of a reference unconditional flow field.
We also propose an
action imagination
scheme: we use “imagined actions” sampled from the unconditional policy, and their advantage estimates, to train the advantage-conditioned policy under a broader action distribution for each state.
The resulting algorithm,
Advantage Guidance
, significantly improves the policy’s ability to respond to advantage inputs, and can target the KL-regularized optimal policy during sampling. Across
26
26
long-horizon, sparse reward tasks with both play-style and demonstration datasets in the offline RL setting, Advantage Guidance outperforms prior strong RL algorithms.

Experiments
We conduct experiments to analyze the empirical effectiveness of Advantage Guidance on a range of long-horizon, sparse reward manipulation tasks.
Concretely, we study the following research questions:
(1)
How well does Advantage Guidance perform compared to prior RL methods on datasets with varying degrees of optimality?
(2)
Do residual parameterization and action imagination improve advantage alignment and policy performance?
(3)
Does contrastive guidance improve policy performance compared to CFG or no guidance?
Additionally, we conduct further ablation experiments in
Section
A.2
. All detailed results are documented in
Section
A.10
.

We evaluate all methods in the offline RL setting with

OGBench offers a suite of long-horizon challenging manipulation tasks, and OCBench is a recently proposed extension of OGBench that provides a more realistic action distribution meant to emulate the statistical properties of real-world human demonstrations.
In particular, the two benchmarks differ substantially in their offline dataset composition.
OGBench is a standard offline RL benchmark with
play-style
datasets generated by scripted behaviors pursuing random goals, often yielding highly suboptimal trajectories for the task objective.
OCBench offers
demonstration-based
datasets, consisting of trajectories generated by near-expert policies with high success rates on the task objective.
Compared to play-style datasets, these demonstrations cover narrower states and predominantly near-optimal actions, making it more challenging for offline RL because extrapolation errors are harder to avoid.
However, such data more closely resembles real-world robotics datasets, and OCBench’s design to emulate human demonstration statistics makes it particularly relevant.

8
Discussions
We demonstrated in this paper that Advantage Guidance can outperform more complex RL methods with a simple supervised learning objective with advantage conditioning and contrastive diffusion guidance during inference. Our work serves as a step towards simple, stable, yet performant off-policy RL algorithms. There are several promising directions for future research. First, our implementation uses a straightforward advantage estimate. While we find this to be empirically effective, a natural next step is to explore whether more intricate advantage estimates improve policy performance, and how policy extraction can be robust in case of noisy advantage estimates. Second, our approach uses contrastive guidance to maximize advantage during inference time, but too large a guidance weight usually lead to a decline in performance. Developing techniques to stably utilize larger guidance weights can further improve the performance of Advantage Guidance. Finally, it would be interesting to explore Advantage Guidance in (offline-to-)online RL settings.

A.4
Does A More Expressive Architecture Help with Advantage Alignment?
In this section, we investigate whether we can improve advantage alignment, and in turn policy performance, of naïve advantage conditioning by using a more expressive conditional policy architecture.
Specifically, we experiment with using a transformer architecture to ingest the conditional advantage.
We compare RCP-A, which uses a FiLM-like architecture that uses the advantage input to modulate the hidden states at every layer of the policy network, to a variant that instead uses a transformer to handle conditional inputs.
We represent each action position in the
H
=
5
H=5
action chunk with a separate token. These action tokens, together with an advantage token, an observation token, and a flow-time token, are processed jointly through self-attention. Each contextualized action token is then projected directly to the velocity vector for its corresponding action position. We use four transformer blocks with model width 256, eight attention heads (32 dimensions per head), and feed-forward width 1024. The FiLM RCP-A actor has approximately
1.39
1.39
M parameters, while the transformer actor has approximately
3.23
3.23
M parameters.

Figure
14

In comparison, Advantage Guidance is much more responsive to different advantage inputs.

article.headline: 优势引导：监督学习损失跑赢离线强化学习
article.lede: 新方法 Advantage Guidance 用优势条件监督学习加对比引导，在 26 个长程稀疏奖励任务上超过 EDP、
article.problem: 以优势值为条件的监督学习（advantage conditioning）理论上能把策略优化变成稳定的模仿学习，但实际中朴素的优势条件策略常常几乎忽略条件输入：论文测得，在条件为真实优势与随机优势时，策略损失的梯度余弦相似度接近 1。作者把这一现象称为「优势对齐问题」——要求高优势时，生成动作的实际优势往往低于请求值。论文还推导出，若直接对连续优势条件策略套用无分类器引导（CFG），得到的分布只会「匹配」某个目标优势值，并同时惩罚高于和低于该值的动作，而不是像 KL 正则最优策略那样单调偏向高优势动作。
article.method: 作者提出 Advantage Guidance（AG）：训练阶段保持简单的监督学习目标，把条件策略参数化为无条件参考流场之上的残差流，让网络把容量集中在优势条件上；同时用「动作想象」为每个状态补充 K 个来自参考策略的采样动作及其优势估计，缓解数据中每个状态只有一个动作、缺乏反事实监督的问题。采样阶段提出「对比引导」：用一对对比条件 (y+, y−) 的条件速度差替代 CFG 的单一条件项，在条件分布属于指数族时，可证明其得分函数精确匹配 π̂(a|s)exp(A(s,a)/β) 这一 KL 正则最优策略。优势估计本身不是贡献点，实验中统一用 IQL 学 Q 和 V，取 A = Q − V。
article.results: 在 20 个 OGBench 任务与 6 个 OCBench 任务、共 26 个长程稀疏奖励任务上，用 10 个随机种子评测：puzzle-3x3 任务平均成功率 AG 为 79.3，EDP 63.8、QGF 63.3、FQL 46.3，而 CFGRL 与 RCP-A 仅 1.5 和 2.9；OCBench 上 block-single 为 95.0 对 EDP 79.5，chamber-easy 为 70.0 对 CFGRL 61.8、EDP 54.6。消融显示想象动作数 K=3 会掉点、K=7 后基本饱和；σ_y 与对比条件 (y+,y−) 在配套调整引导权重后影响很小。与 best-of-N 采样相比，AG 在 OGBench 小 N 时领先且测试算力更少，但 N 足够大时略逊于 BFN；在 OCBench 上即使 N 很大 AG 仍明显更好。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明策略提取未必需要 actor-critic 式的迭代优化与 Q 梯度反传：保留监督学习的稳定结构，再加一个可证明指向 KL 正则最优策略的采样期引导，就能在长程稀疏奖励任务上达到甚至超过专用离线 RL 方法。
article.limitations: 结论建立在 IQL 给出的优势估计上，论文未评测优势噪声或更复杂估计器下的稳健性；引导权重过大反而掉点，作者也承认尚缺稳定使用大权重的办法。此外对比引导在 OGBench 上与 CFG、纯条件采样表现相近，优势主要体现在 OCBench 这类窄分布的示范数据上，且全部实验限于离线设定，未涉及在线或离线到在线。

page_papers.title: In-Distribution Forcing for Long Video Generation at Test Time
page_papers.abstract: Modern autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models excel at short-horizon video generation, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to drifting, where colors and textures shift, and motion dynamics decay. Existing works primarily rely on KV conditioning, which selects or modifies cached key-value (KV) entries to mitigate drifting. However, we observe that KV conditioning alone is insufficient as it assumes cached KV entries remain in-distribution. This assumption fails beyond the training horizon: nothing constrains the construction of KV entries during rollout, giving rise to the KV-provenance problem where cached entries themselves become out-of-distribution (OOD). To address this, we propose In-Distribution Forcing (ID-Forcing), a test-time framework that aligns both KV caching and KV conditioning with training configurations. Its key mechanism, self-caching, prevents OOD KV entries at their source. Each chunk is cached without attending to prior KV entry, keeping the rolling window exactly in-distribution. Consequently, ID-Forcing seamlessly extends short-horizon models to minute-scale video generation. Extensive evaluations show that our method remains competitive on standard video generation benchmark while substantially outperforming prior work in mitigating drifting, as validated by both our drift metrics and a user study.

Abstract
Modern autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models excel at short-horizon video generation, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to
drifting
, where colors and textures shift, and motion dynamics decay. Existing works primarily rely on
KV conditioning
, which selects or modifies cached key-value (KV) entries to mitigate drifting. However, we observe that KV conditioning alone is insufficient as it assumes cached KV entries remain in-distribution. This assumption fails beyond the training horizon: nothing constrains the construction of KV entries during rollout, giving rise to the
KV-provenance problem
where cached entries themselves become out-of-distribution (OOD). To address this, we propose
In-Distribution Forcing (ID-Forcing)
, a test-time framework that aligns both KV caching and KV conditioning with training configurations.
Its key mechanism,
self-caching
, prevents OOD KV entries at their source. Each chunk is cached without attending to prior KV entry, keeping the rolling window exactly in-distribution.
Consequently, ID-Forcing seamlessly extends short-horizon models to minute-scale video generation. Extensive evaluations show that our method remains competitive on standard video generation benchmark while substantially outperforming prior work in mitigating drifting, as validated by both our drift metrics and a user study.

1
Introduction
Recent advances in video diffusion models
(
Google DeepMind, 2025
;
Kling Team, Kuaishou Technology, 2025
;
OpenAI, 2025
;
Wan et al., 2025
)
enable high-fidelity synthesis of short video clips with coherent motion,
yet interactive applications such as world models
(
Hong et al., 2025
;
Shen et al., 2026
;
Huang et al., 2025a
)
, streaming content
(
Kodaira et al., 2026
;
Henschel et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
, and long-form storytelling
(
Elmoghany et al., 2026
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
demand generation far beyond a few seconds. To enable such long-horizon generation, autoregressive (AR) video diffusion
(
Yin et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2025b
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
has emerged as the standard paradigm, generating videos sequentially in chunks while conditioning each new chunk on the key–value (KV) cache of previously generated content. Specifically, Self-Forcing
(
Huang et al., 2025b
)
reduces the training-inference gap by
training on autoregressive rollouts, while LongLive
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
extends generation to longer horizons through streaming long-video tuning.
However, the ability to generate over extended horizons does not ensure that visual quality persists. As generation proceeds, colors and textures tend to shift, and motion dynamics gradually decay. This progressive degradation, known as
drifting
, arises because the rollout at inference differs from the rollout seen during training.
Training on self-rollouts
(
Huang et al., 2025b
;
Cui et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
addresses this by exposing the model to its own generated context, but only within a finite training horizon. Extrapolating beyond this horizon therefore introduces conditioning configurations outside the training distribution, causing errors to accumulate over time. Yet simply extending the training horizon cannot solve this issue, as extrapolating past the horizon is inherently unavoidable in arbitrarily long video generation.
To address drifting, a large body of work controls what the model reads from the KV cache during generation, which we refer to as
KV conditioning
.
Existing approaches typically select cached entries at the chunk level, as with attention sinks
(
Yi et al., 2026
)
, or modify their temporal positional embeddings
(
Yesiltepe et al., 2026
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
These methods, however, are valid only under the assumption that the cached KV entries are in-distribution, as they consider only which entries to attend to and where to position them.
This assumption has not been explicitly examined, and nothing ensures that it holds.
Thus, understanding drifting requires examining not only the KV entries read during generation, but also the context under which they were constructed.
We observe that whether a KV entry is in-distribution is determined by
KV caching
, the operation that computes and stores a KV entry for each generated chunk.
A KV entry depends not only on its own chunk but also on the other KV entries it attends to during KV caching,
i.e.,
its
provenance
.
Beyond the training horizon, every chunk is cached under a provenance never seen during training, so the resulting KV entry is out-of-distribution.
We term this the
KV-provenance problem
(
Fig.
2
).
Since provenance is fixed at KV caching, no KV conditioning policy can recover from it, and keeping extrapolation in-distribution requires controlling
both KV caching and KV conditioning
.
Motivated by this insight, we propose
In-Distribution Forcing (ID-Forcing)
, a test-time method that aligns both KV caching and KV conditioning with the KV context configurations encountered during training.
For KV caching, we introduce
self-caching
.
Beyond the training horizon, the earlier KV entries are cached attending only to themselves, while the later ones are cached autoregressively on top of them, which prevents any unseen provenance from being constructed (§
3.1
).
For KV conditioning, we show that the first chunk must remain in the conditioning window for it to stay in-distribution, and that self-caching keeps the rolling window exactly in-distribution (§
3.2
).
Every KV operation is thus one that training executed.
As a result, our method yields a remarkably simple framework:
a plain rolling window with one rule for each KV operation, extending a five-second model to minute-scale generation.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We characterize the
KV-provenance problem
as a source of drift in long-video extrapolation and establish the importance of keeping both KV caching and KV conditioning within the configurations encountered during training (§
3.1
).
•
We propose
In-Distribution Forcing (ID-Forcing)
, which introduces
self-caching
to control cache provenance and jointly aligns KV caching and KV conditioning with training (§
3.1
, §
3.2
).
•
We demonstrate effective suppression of drift in minute-scale generation, preserving visual quality and temporal consistency while maintaining active motion (§
4
).

4.2
Main Results
Quantitative Results.
Tab.
1
reports VBench-Long
(
Huang et al., 2024
)
metrics for 120- and 240-second videos, built on top of two base models. Compared with all baselines, ID-Forcing achieves substantial gains on both drift metrics, indicating that visual quality and motion dynamics remain stable over long durations. This resistance to motion degradation is further shown by Dynamic Degree, where our method achieves the highest score in every setting. In contrast, base models such as Self-Forcing and LongLive exhibit markedly lower dynamic degree, particularly at longer durations, reflecting a tendency toward frame freezing as generation extends.
Notably, our method also performs well on Aesthetic Quality, Imaging Quality, and Subject Consistency. The one exception is Motion Smoothness, which measures local frame-to-frame stability and is therefore inherently biased toward methods with lower dynamic degree; on all other metrics, ID-Forcing remains competitive with or superior to the baselines. This result suggests that our method mitigates long-horizon drift without sacrificing generation quality.
Qualitative Results.
Fig.
4
shows qualitative comparisons on 2-minute video generation. On the Self-Forcing base model, the base model itself suffers severe color and motion collapse over time. Adding Deep Forcing stabilizes color but subject consistency still degrades, with the puppies’ identities gradually drifting. ∞-RoPE exhibits color saturation alongside a similar loss of subject consistency, while MemRoPE shows unnatural color shifts and changing textures across frames. In contrast, ID-Forcing remains stable throughout, preserving both subject consistency and color fidelity.
On the LongLive base model, color drift is generally less severe across all methods, but subject consistency remains a challenge: the base model shows the subject’s clothing color changing over time. Deep Forcing suppresses motion and introduces color artifacts, including unnatural brightening and a bluish tint. Both ∞-RoPE and MemRoPE exhibit highly inconsistent motion throughout generation. ID-Forcing, by contrast, maintains subject consistency, sustains motion until the end of the sequence, and preserves accurate color throughout.

Qualitative ablation on 2-minute video.
Components are added from top to bottom. Without self-caching, colors and textures still drift even with the sink and re-rotation, whereas the full ID-Forcing preserves the scene and color throughout the 2-minute video.
We ablate the three components of ID-Forcing: self-caching for KV caching, and, for KV conditioning, retaining the first chunk as a sink and re-rotating the window into the trained positional range.
As shown in
Fig.
5

Retaining the first chunk largely stabilizes generation, consistent with the known empirical effect of attention sinks, but colors and textures still drift, frames flicker, and the video periodically resets to an earlier scene.
Adding re-rotation improves this further, yet drifting persists, as KV caching remains out-of-distribution.
Self-caching brings KV caching in-distribution as well, greatly reducing color and texture drifting while preserving the dynamics.

5
Related Works
Video Diffusion Models.
Video diffusion models with bidirectional attention produce high-quality clips
(
OpenAI, 2025
;
Wan et al., 2025
;
Kong et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
, but attend over the entire sequence at once, so their cost grows quadratically with length and the output length is fixed at sampling time.
Autoregressive (AR) formulations instead factorize the video into chunks generated in sequence, each conditioned on the KV cache of its predecessors
(
Chen et al., 2024
;
Yin et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2025b
)
.
This makes the cost linear, admits streaming output, and in principle allows a video of arbitrary length to be produced at test time.
The AR factorization, however, feeds each chunk back as the condition for the next, so any deviation from the training distribution accumulates along the rollout, a failure known as
drifting
(
Chen et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2025b
)
.
Addressing Drifting in AR Video Diffusion.
The most straightforward way is to train on longer contexts
(
Cui et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Teng et al., 2025
)
.
However, this does not remove the boundary, since training always covers a fixed horizon while the AR formulation exists to continue past whatever length was trained. Moreover, this is infeasible with extremely long videos since the cost of extending that horizon during training grows with the target length.
A test-time extrapolation method is therefore necessary regardless of how the model was trained, and the two directions are orthogonal: a better-trained backbone still requires a rule for what to do beyond its horizon.
Test-time methods approach this by managing the KV cache during generation.
Deep Forcing
(
Yi et al., 2026
)
keeps early KV entries as sinks, realigns their temporal RoPE to the current timeline, and compresses the rest.
∞
\infty
-RoPE
(
Yesiltepe et al., 2026
)
reassigns temporal indices so that the offsets seen at inference stay within the trained range.
MemRoPE
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
caches keys without rotation and aggregates evicted entries into memory tokens, applying RoPE online at attention time.
All of these act on
KV conditioning
, leaving untouched how each KV entry was written.
In contrast, we address both
KV caching
and
KV conditioning
, keeping test-time extrapolation within the training distribution.
6
Conclusion
In this paper, we introduce
In-Distribution Forcing
, a training-free framework designed to enable stable long-horizon video generation. By analyzing the autoregressive (AR) model’s key-value (KV) dynamics, we identify the
KV-provenance problem
: a critical out-of-distribution (OOD) failure mode originating at the caching level. To resolve this, we propose a two-level KV management rule: at the caching level, we apply self-caching for KV caching; at the conditioning level, we strictly bound the window length (
L
≤
N
−
1
L\leq N{-}1
) while permanently fixing the first chunk
κ
0
\kappa_{0}
. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our method achieves highly competitive performance across diverse durations, backbones, and metrics. Most importantly, our framework effectively addresses the quality drift issue inherent to autoregressive models, maintaining stable video dynamics even over minute-scale generations.

article.headline: 长视频漂移的源头在KV缓存写入
article.lede: ID-Forcing 无需额外训练，在测试时同时约束 KV 缓存与 KV 条件选择，把 5 秒模型延到分钟级。
article.problem: 自回归视频扩散模型在训练时域之外生成时会出现漂移：颜色和纹理逐渐偏移，运动动态衰减。现有测试时方法几乎都只改「KV 条件」，即挑选或调整要读取哪些缓存条目，却默认被缓存的 KV 条目本身仍在训练分布内。作者指出这个假设在超出训练时域后必然失效：每个 chunk 的 KV 条目是在训练中从未见过的上下文里写入的，他们称之为 KV-provenance 问题。
article.method: 作者提出 ID-Forcing，一个免训练的两级 KV 管理框架。第一级是 self-caching：在条件窗口里，前 ℓ 个条目只依赖自身写入（不 attend 任何先前 KV），其余条目在它们之上自回归写入，从而让每个条目的写入上下文都落在训练见过的配置内。第二级是条件规则：首个 chunk κ0 因因果 3D-VAE 对首帧的编码方式在分布上不可替代，需永久保留在 slot 0，其余取最近 L−1 个条目并整体做 R−f 重旋转，使窗口内每个时间距离都与训练一致。
article.results: 在 Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B 上以 Self-Forcing 和 LongLive 为基座，用 128 条 MovieGen prompt、480×832 分辨率评测。以 Self-Forcing 为基座的 120 秒视频上，ID-Forcing 的 Color Drift 为 72.37、Motion Drift 为 89.06、Dynamic Degree 为 65.65，而 Self-Forcing 本身分别为 25.54、46.88、30.04，MemRoPE 为 59.25、82.81、62.90；240 秒时三项为 70.34、92.19、64.76（Self-Forcing 为 20.98、56.25、29.61）。消融显示加入 self-caching 后 Color Drift 从 60.66 升至 72.37，Aesthetic Quality 从 54.14 升至 58.23。20 人、20 条 prompt 的 2AFC 用户研究中，总体偏好率相对 Self-Forcing 为 100.0%、Deep Forcing 95.0%、∞-RoPE 93.0%、MemRoPE 86.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把长视频漂移的归因从「读什么」扩展到「怎么写」，说明只改 KV 条件选择无法挽回在写入阶段就已出分布的缓存。这一视角对所有基于滚动窗口的自回归视频模型都适用，且方法本身不需要重新训练。
article.limitations: 实验只在一个 1.3B 骨干（Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B）、固定 480×832 分辨率和 128 条 prompt 上验证，泛化性未证；两个漂移指标（HSV 直方图 L1 距离、首尾 5 秒 Dynamic Degree 差）由作者自行定义并校准，非第三方标准。此外论文自己也承认 Motion Smoothness 上不占优（如 120 秒 Self-Forcing 基座下 97.77，低于 Self-Forcing 的 98.26），而在 LongLive 240 秒的 Motion Drift 上为 96.09，略低于 MemRoPE 的 96.88，说明对已长时训练的基座收益更有限。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图中对比两种方案的 KV 操作：左侧 Self-Forcing 对每个条目都自回归缓存，超出训练时域后条目是在训练未见过的窗口下写入；右侧 ID-Forcing 让靠前的条目自缓存、其余在其上自回归，使每个条目的写入窗口都落在训练分布内。

figure.caption: {KV operations comparison.} Both illustrations show the caching window of each KV entry and the conditioning window of size $L$ used to generate chunk $x_i$. {Left}: Self-Forcing caches every entry autoregressively, so entries beyond the horizon are cached under windows unseen in training. {Right}: ID-Forcing caches the earlier entries with self-caching and the rest autoregressively on top of them, so every entry is cached under a window seen in training.

page_papers.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
page_papers.abstract: Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints. Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials. Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower. Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or MuJoCo's signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at https://younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/.
page_papers.content:
Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive
Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
Antonia Bronars
†
†
thanks:
Equal contribution.
Younghyo Park
1
1
footnotemark:
1
Kushal Kedia
Pulkit Agrawal
Affiliation:
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract
Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints.
Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body
motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must
find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light
contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe
only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without
visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part
are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must
therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own
proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over
randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear
meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real
world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials.
Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower.
Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each
simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an
open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces
for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or
MuJoCo’s signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at
younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/
.
1
Introduction
A force applied anywhere on a robot’s body travels through its links to the
joints, which then move differently from what their commands alone would
produce. The encoders record that difference, so the joints of every arm and
leg double as contact sensors. Legged robots exploit this proprioceptive
signal to walk, run, and climb stairs blind
(
Lee et al., 2020
;
Siekmann et al., 2021a
;
Siekmann et al., 2021b
;
Kumar et al., 2021
)
,
and humanoids to walk and track whole-body motions
(
Radosavovic et al., 2024
;
Cheng et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2024
)
. In these
settings, however, contacts are large and forceful, and joints often comply meaningfully while recording measurable deviations. Can robots exploit the same signal for precise, contact-rich assembly?
Precise assembly with a robotic arm occupies the opposite regime: the robot must
find an opening with a millimeter or less of clearance, bring gear teeth into mesh, or
catch a thread, through light contact whose effect on the joints is easy to miss. We
study this question by training
blind
assembly policies that have no
information outside of their own joint sensing, and verify that proprioception
contains enough information for three such tasks: peg insertion, gear meshing, and
nut threading (figure
2
). In the real world, our peg insertion policy
inserts eight pegs of different cross-sections, three of them outside
its training distribution, with 0.5–1.5 mm of clearance per side, in
73% of 237 trials, without being
given the hole’s location, the peg’s pose in its grasp, the part’s size, or
its clearance (section
3.4
). To our knowledge,
this is the first such demonstration.
We train our policies entirely in simulation with reinforcement learning and
deploy the peg insertion policy in the real world without fine-tuning
(figure
1
). Training
randomizes part geometry, contact properties, fixture poses, and grasps, which can
hold the part off-center on the finger pads and tilted in the grasp. The policy
observes a 0.6 s history of joint positions and velocities, the gripper
pose and twist computed from them, and its own previous actions. It receives
no image and no force signal, so it can perceive contact and find the hole, shaft,
or bolt only through its own motion (section
2
).
Figure 1:
Blind insertion.
A policy trained only in simulation
inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in the real world using only its
joint encoders and previous actions.
On all three tasks, probing the blind policies’ learned representations and comparing them with matched visual policies revealed two interesting properties of visually blind behaviors:
•
Visually blind yet intelligent.
The learned behavior is not an open-loop pattern: its learned representation encoding its own proprioceptive inputs contains meaningful task-relevant information that the policy itself heavily relies on to adjust its behavior (section
3.2
).
•
Proprioception generalizes better.
Because a blind policy depends on the part only through its contacts, it degrades far less than vision on part shapes and sizes it has not seen during training (section
3.3
).
Training for this robustness requires diverse parts: thousands of different
assemblies, generated procedurally and simulated in parallel, each with its
millimeter clearance intact. In MuJoCo
(
Todorov et al., 2012
)
, building
holes from convex primitives by hand does not scale to random shapes, and the
automatic alternatives, convex decomposition and signed-distance-field (SDF)
collision, are less accurate and slower at these clearances. We therefore
built
mjfit
, which procedurally generates pegs and holes from any planar outline, as well as threads and gears, out of exact convex prisms. To summarize, our contributions are:
1.
Blind policies, trained purely in simulation, that learn peg insertion,
gear meshing, and nut threading from proprioception alone, given no fixture pose,
grasp, or part model
(section
3.1
), with analyses showing that
on all three tasks they search reactively,
acting on the contact state their joint histories encode rather than following a
fixed pattern (section
3.2
), and that they generalize to unseen part shapes and
sizes better than matched visual policies (section
3.3
);
2.
The first sim-to-real policy for precise insertion from proprioception alone:
trained only in simulation, the peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to a real
robot and inserts pegs of different cross-sections, including pegs outside its
training distribution (section
3.4
);
3.
mjfit
, an open-source procedural generator of assemblies for MuJoCo
(pegs and holes, threads, and gears) with exact convex collision geometry,
which supplies the thousands of different training assemblies, and a
benchmark against analytic ground truth in which it is more accurate and
faster than convex decomposition and MuJoCo’s SDF collision
(section
2.2
).
2
Learning blind assembly
We train blind policies for three assemblies that
mjfit
generates: peg insertion, gear
meshing, and nut threading. We describe the tasks (section
2.1
); how
mjfit
, our
open-source procedural generator for MuJoCo, supplies thousands of different
assemblies with exact convex collision geometry that preserves their clearances
(section
2.2
); and the policy, whose auxiliary contact supervision makes learning
faster without giving the actor any privileged information
(section
2.3
; figure
14
).
2.1
Tasks
Figure 2:
Peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading.
(a–c) A start of
each task, faded, and the same grasp at success: the peg seated in
its hole, the gear seated on its shaft in mesh with both anchor gears, and the nut
turned until its thread has caught. (d–f) Stadium pegs, gear sets, and nuts and
bolts generated by
mjfit
and used for training, to scale.
Figure 3:
Training fixture poses and grasps.
Gear and bolt fixtures span
the peg’s ranges.
In all three tasks (figure
2
), a 7-DOF robot arm equipped with a parallel jaw gripper holds a part
and must assemble it with a fixture that can sit almost anywhere in its workspace, and tilted (figure
3
a). The part’s geometry, its
pose in the grasp (figure
3
b), and the contact properties are randomized and not observed by policy (Table
1
). Episodes
start with the part touching the fixture but misaligned, and succeed once it is
fully assembled. This requires the policy to both search for alignment through contact, and then perform the assembly, based on its joint position feedback alone.
•
Peg insertion:
the pegs are prisms with varying cross-section, size,
aspect ratio, mass, and length, with 1.0–1.5 mm of clearance per side
(Appendix
A
). Pegs start typically around 2 cm from the hole,
tilted far more than the clearance admits, and succeed when the peg is seated in the
hole.
•
Gear meshing:
spur gears of varying size and tooth count must slide down a
shaft into mesh with one or two anchor gears that turn on their own axles, with
0.2–0.6 mm of backlash. Episodes start with the gear in contact with the shaft tip, but misaligned and with its teeth out of phase with the anchors’, and succeed when the gear
is seated on the shaft with teeth meshed.
•
Nut threading:
metric nuts from M24 to M42 must thread onto a bolt with 0.05–0.2 mm of thread clearance. Episodes start with the nut resting on the bolt’s
tip, off its axis and tilted, and succeed a quarter turn after the thread catches.
2.2
Simulating tight insertion at scale
Training on this distribution means simulating thousands of parallel worlds
that each hold a different, randomly generated assembly, with per-side
clearances down to 0.5 mm. MuJoCo collides meshes
through their convex hulls, so a concave hole must be given an SDF or built
from convex pieces, which simulation benchmarks assemble from boxes by hand
(
Zhu et al., 2020
;
Tao et al., 2024
;
Zakka et al., 2025
)
.
Figure 4:
Assets generated by
mjfit
one color per convex
piece of the generated collision geometry. Labels give the number of convex pieces (pcs) and the CPU time per
physics step with the parts in contact.
Exact convex decomposition.
mjfit
automates the hand-built hole
and generalizes it to arbitrary outlines. Given the planar outline of a hole,
optionally with islands such as connector pins, it emits a ready-to-simulate
MJCF model in which every contact surface is a MuJoCo primitive or a convex
prism (figure
4
). The plate around the hole is split into convex
polygons and extruded; the peg is the hole outline offset inward by the
clearance, so every peg edge sits exactly the clearance from its hole edge,
and islands become pockets in a hollow peg. Curves are tessellated by a
circumscribed
polygon, so the wall never intrudes into the true hole,
as it does in rings of boxes that inscribe the circle
(
Zhu et al., 2020

2.3
Policy and training
Policy.
At each step, the actor (figure
7
) observes its
joint positions and velocities, the gripper pose and twist computed from them
by forward kinematics, and its previous action. It never receives the hole
pose, the part geometry, a wrench estimate, or an image. A temporal
convolutional encoder compresses the last 0.6 s of observations into a
latent, and an MLP maps the latent and the current observation to
joint-position increments. A joint impedance controller tracks them on an arm model
whose armature, damping, and friction were identified from real-world measurements.
Additional training details in Appendix
A
.
Training.
We use PPO
(
Schulman et al., 2017
)
with a sparse
reward: a bonus on success and one-time bonuses for intermediate milestones, such
as the peg’s first capture by the opening (Appendix
A.1
gives the
gear’s and nut’s). Two training-only signals speed up learning from the sparse reward
without giving the actor privileged information: an asymmetric critic
(
Pinto et al., 2018
)
that also sees the part’s pose relative to the fixture
and the true contact labels, and the contact supervision described next.

A blind policy has to infer contact from how
the arm moves. To give that inference a dense training signal, we supervise

3
Results
We design experiments to answer the following questions:
1.
(section
3.1
) Can a policy that senses only its own joints learn precise assembly tasks including peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading?
2.
(section
3.2
) Do blind policies learn intelligent, contact-reactive search, or is it learning scripted patterns?
3.
(section
3.3
) Do blind policies generalize better than visual policies to part geometries outside the training distribution?
4.
(section
3.4
) Can blind policies that rely on contact-rich search be transferred zero shot with high fidelity to the real world?
3.1
Proprioception is sufficient
Figure 8:
Proprioception alone is enough to learn all three tasks.
Blind
policies, which sense only their own joints, reach the same near-perfect training
success as visual policies with a wrist camera. Lines are the mean of two training seeds.
All three tasks achieve near-perfect success on in-distribution geometries (figure
11
, left). The joint history alone therefore carries enough information about contact to find an
opening, bring teeth into mesh, and engage a thread.
Compared with visual policies, which can typically observe the poses of the grasped and mating parts directly, blind policies may be slower. On peg insertion, the blind
policy has to search for the opening through contact, so
it takes a less direct path and seats later (figure
9
a, b) than a visual policy. The gap is
smaller on the other two tasks (Appendix
C
), plausibly because the grasped part occludes more of the mating part from the camera’s view, so the visual policy, too, has to search to some extent.
Figure 9:

Because the blind policy must search through contact, it follows a less direct path and seats later than the visual policy (a, b). Nonetheless, it travels far less (c) than an optimistic scripted spiral search baseline
(
Chhatpar & Branicky, 2001
)
.

Reacting to contacts also makes a blind assembly efficient. A fixed pattern
sweeps the same path regardless of what the arm feels, whereas a reactive policy can use the information gathered through contact, such as the peg catching the rim of the opening, to steer its
search. We test this on peg insertion, where a scripted blind baseline is standard:

;

spiral that starts flush with the hole opening, and is given the peg’s orientation and the best starting direction
(figure
9

3.3
Generalization to unseen parts
Figure 11:
Proprioceptive policies remain more robust to geometric variation.
Success of the
blind and visual policies (both with a 30-step history) on each task, in
distribution (left of the dashed line) and on unseen parts, each widening one
object property beyond its training range while the others stay within
theirs.
On all three tasks, both blind policies and visual policies are
reliable on the parts they were trained on. However, the blind policy is more reliable on assemblies sampled from outside the training distribution (figure
11
). The visual policy is particularly vulnerable to geometry changes that significantly change how the parts look; it consistently underperforms the blind policy across tasks when evaluated on parts that are of a different shape, or extremely different size, than the training distribution. The visual policy learns to align visual features which may not appear in held-out assemblies. The blind policy, on the other hand, learns a searching strategy that is much more transferable.
3.4
Zero-shot transfer to the real world
Setup.
We deploy the frozen blind policy on a Flexiv Rizon 4S with
a Robotiq 2F-85 at 50 Hz, with no real-world data or fine-tuning. It receives
only encoder-derived joint and gripper state; no camera, force/torque sensor,
or hole pose enters the policy. The deployed policy is a policy
trained on random convex, smooth, and mixed cross-sections under a handle
(Table
2
). We test eight 3D-printed pegs (figure
12
): five
in-distribution objects, and three that are drawn from outside the training distribution, a tighter clearance (0.5 mm per side), a larger cross-section, and a
taller handle. Each trial starts from a
start state drawn from the simulated reset distribution, with the peg grasped
at a randomized position and tilt and touching the fixture near the hole. An operator marks a
trial as successful once the peg is seated.
