Results.
One policy, with no parameter changes, succeeds in
173 of 237 trials (73%; figure
12
), pressing onto
the surface, sweeping, and dropping in once the opening is under the peg, as in
simulation (figure
1
). It succeeds in 73–80% of trials on each
in-distribution peg, and in 66%, 66%, and 72% on the tighter, larger, and
taller-handled pegs, respectively.
4
Related work
Robotic insertion.
Classical peg-in-hole assembly combines
compliance with search patterns such as spirals, rasters, and tilting
(
Whitney, 1982
;
Chhatpar & Branicky, 2001
;
Marvel et al., 2018
)
, in
some cases without force feedback
(
Park et al., 2017
)
; these
strategies assume a known grasp and a hole within the pattern and are tuned
for each part. Learned insertion policies usually add force/torque sensing
(
Inoue et al., 2017
;
Beltran-Hernandez et al., 2020
)
, wrist vision
(
Schoettler et al., 2020
;
Bogunowicz et al., 2020
;
Spector & Di Castro, 2021
;
Haugaard et al., 2021
;
Seo et al., 2025
)
,
or both
(
Lee et al., 2019
;
Luo et al., 2021
;
Watson et al., 2020
)
. Wrist force/torque sensing combined with a soft wrist has allowed policies to tolerate 10 mm of
hole-position error and an unseen peg shape
(
Fuchioka et al., 2024
)
,
while a blind dexterous policy relying on fingertip tactile sensing
(
Pan et al.,
)
was demonstrated for precise insertion. Others
(
Tang et al., 2023
;
Tang et al., 2024
;
Noseworthy et al., 2025
;
Narang et al., 2022
)
observe joint
state and a direct goal pose from perception or calibration with a few millimeters
of error. Our policy instead uses proprioception alone: it is given no
hole pose, part model, or force signal, and must locate the hole through
contact while the peg’s pose in its grasp is unknown.
Proprioceptive policies.
Legged robots traverse rough terrain
with policies built on histories of onboard state
(
Hwangbo et al., 2019
;
Lee et al., 2020
;
Siekmann et al., 2021b
;
Kumar et al., 2021
;
Radosavovic et al., 2024
)
.
In manipulation, proprioceptive policies reorient unseen objects in hand
(
Chen et al., 2021
;
Qi et al., 2022
)
, and
Blind Dexterity
treats
joint and action histories as a whole-body tactile channel
(
Bhatt et al., 2026
)
. These tasks involve forceful contact or
centimeter tolerances; insertion needs neither. In imitation learning, robot state can hurt
(
Team et al., 2024
)
by suppressing visual learning
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
.
Simulating tight contact.
Approximate convex decomposition
(
Mamou & Ghorbel, 2009
;
Wei et al., 2022
)
tolerates concavity relative to the mesh
size, which can exceed an assembly’s clearance. Exact polygon partitions are
classical
(
Keil, 1985
)
, and simulation benchmarks build holes
from primitives by hand
(
Zhu et al., 2020
;
Tao et al., 2024
;
Zakka et al., 2025
)
;
mjfit
automates this for arbitrary outlines and generates assemblies in bulk. SDFs
handle concavity directly and underlie GPU assembly simulation in Factory and
its successors
(
Narang et al., 2022
;
Macklin et al., 2020
;
Tang et al., 2023
)
,
whose assets obtain their clearance approximately, by displacing mesh vertices
or eroding voxels
(
Tang et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2025
)
; SDF accuracy
depends on field resolution and contact search. Newton combines SDFs with
hydroelastic contact
(
The Newton developers, 2025
)
, and barrier methods simulate threads and
gear trains without interpenetration
(
Ferguson et al., 2021
;
Lan et al., 2022
)
. Our benchmark (section
2.2
)
follows the simulator comparisons of
Erez et al. (2015)
and
Le Lidec et al. (2024)
. CRISP
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
recently compared
engines on tight insertion and threading; we instead keep MuJoCo’s solver
fixed and vary only the collision geometry, using passive probes with analytic
answers and speed–accuracy Pareto fronts.
5
Limitations and conclusion
We trained blind policies that insert pegs, mesh gears, and thread nuts from
proprioception alone, with no fixture pose, grasp, or part model, on thousands of
assemblies that
mjfit
generates with exact collision geometry. The peg insertion
policy transfers zero-shot to the real world, and in simulation, blind policies
generalize to unseen parts far better than matched visual policies. The peg
insertion policy is, however, a last-mile manipulation skill, and its limits are
those of one. First, it assumes it starts in contact: every training episode
begins with the peg already touching the fixture a few centimeters from the
hole, so another motion, scripted or visual, must bring it there. Second, its
behavior is local. It searches the surface around where it starts and
corrects the misalignments it met in training, but it cannot handle events
that call for more than a local correction, such as a peg that slides out from the
grasp and lands far from the hole.

Tasks.
Physics runs at 1 kHz under a 50 Hz policy, and each world holds one part and
fixture drawn from
mjfit
’s generators.
Peg insertion:
each episode starts
with the peg touching the fixture’s top face, a median 1 cm from the hole center.
It succeeds when the entire peg bottom face is seated in the hole. Bonuses of
+
1
+1
reward the peg’s first capture by the opening and success. Contact labels mark each
of 64 points on the peg’s bottom edge as free (more than 1 mm above the fixture’s
top face), in contact (on the rim or top face, within 1 mm), or inside the opening.
An episode lasts at most 5 s.
Gear meshing:
each world holds a spur-gear set
from
mjfit
’s gear generator, and the robot holds the gear by a printed boss. Each
episode starts with the gear resting on the shaft tip, off the shaft axis, with its
teeth out of phase with the anchors’. It succeeds when the bore surrounds the shaft
and the gear sits within 1 mm of the shaft’s collar, which the anchors’ teeth allow
only in mesh. Bonuses reward the first capture of the shaft, the first mesh with
every anchor, and success; contact labels mark 64 points on the shaft’s rim (free,
on the gear, or inside the bore) and 64 on the gear’s tooth tips (free, on an
anchor, or in mesh); an episode lasts at most 10 s.
Nut threading:
each
world holds an ISO metric nut and bolt pair from
mjfit
’s thread generator. Each
episode starts with the nut resting on the bolt tip, tilted and off the bolt axis,
short of the turn at which the thread catches it. It succeeds a quarter turn after
the thread catches, with the nut within 1 mm of the bolt axis; bonuses reward
seating, capture, each new extent of the turn, and success; contact labels mark 64
points on the rim of the nut’s bore (free, on the bolt’s tip, around the bolt, or
caught by the thread, within a band of 0.29 pitch, 1 mm at M30
×
\times
3.5); an
episode lasts at most 15 s. Every episode also ends when the part moves far from
the fixture, and a nut episode when the nut leaves the grasp.
Architecture.
The actor observes 33 values per step: seven joint
positions, seven joint velocities, the gripper pose and twist (twelve), and its
previous action (seven). The nut policy’s actor encodes the gripper orientation by
two columns of its rotation matrix rather than by Euler angles (36 values), since
the wrist turns through half a revolution while threading. A temporal convolutional
encoder maps the last 30 observations (0.6 s) to a 32-dimensional latent; an MLP
(256, 256, 128 units) maps the latent and the current observation to seven
joint-position increments, scaled by the action scale of Table
1
and
added to the measured joint positions. The critic sees the part’s pose relative to
the fixture, the contact labels, and, for the nut, the thread’s geometry (240, 434,
and 317 inputs for the peg, gear, and nut).

article.headline: 仅凭关节编码器，盲插销孔真机成功率达73%
article.lede: MIT 团队在仿真中训练只靠本体感知的装配策略，插销任务零样本迁移到真机，237 次试验成功 173 次。
article.problem: 把销钉插进单边间隙约 1 mm 的孔、让齿轮齿入啮合、把螺母拧上螺栓，这类精密装配通常要依赖腕部相机或力/力矩传感器。作者追问：机器人自身的关节编码器——腿足机器人靠它盲走楼梯——是否也足以支撑这种轻接触、毫米级公差的装配？在他们的设定中，夹具位姿、零件在夹爪中的位姿和零件几何都不告诉策略。
article.method: 策略只接收最近 0.6 s（30 步）的关节位置与速度、由正运动学算出的夹爪位姿与速度以及上一步动作，经时间卷积压成隐变量后由 MLP 输出关节位置增量，交给关节阻抗控制器。训练完全在 MuJoCo 中用 PPO 加稀疏奖励完成，并用非对称 critic 和一个接触解码器的辅助交叉熵加速学习；接触预测只训练编码器，从不进入 actor。为在真实间隙下大规模并行仿真，作者开发了开源生成器 mjfit，把任意平面轮廓精确分解为凸棱柱，一次训练可跑 12,288 个各不相同的装配世界。
article.results: 仿真中插销、齿轮啮合、螺母拧入三种任务在训练分布内均接近满分（盲插销策略成功率 99.4%）。真机上冻结的策略零样本完成 237 次试验中的 173 次（73%），五个分布内销钉为 73–80%，更紧配合（单边 0.5 mm）、更大截面、更高手柄的销钉分别为 66%、66%、72%。在未见过的随机凸形销钉上，盲策略成功率 36.2%，匹配的视觉策略仅 3.9%。线性探针从历史隐变量解码任务模式，平衡准确率为 61–73%，高于只看当前观测的 41–64%（随机猜测为 14%）。代价是速度：插销盲策略横向行程中位数 37 mm、入座耗时中位数 0.80 s，视觉策略为 20 mm 和 0.44 s；脚本化螺旋搜索基线的行程为 95 mm。mjfit 在 16 mm 圆孔、100 µm 间隙的基准上，CPU 单线程比网格 SDF 快约一个数量级，精度相当或更好。
article.why_it_matters: 结果表明，机械臂自带的关节编码器在毫米级间隙的接触装配中携带了足够信息，有望省掉相机与力/力矩传感器，降低精密装配的硬件成本；配套的 mjfit 生成器则让成千上万套精确保留间隙的装配体可以批量用于并行仿真训练。
article.limitations: 策略假设起始时已与工件接触：每次训练回合都从销钉已接触夹具、距孔约 1–2 cm 处开始，靠近孔的过程需由其他运动或视觉完成；而且行为是局部的，若销钉从夹爪中滑脱并落到远离孔的位置，它无法处理。真机验证只覆盖插销一项任务，齿轮啮合与螺母拧入仍停留在仿真；接触辅助损失在训练时依赖仿真器的特权状态标注。
article.figure_caption_zh: 策略结构：时间卷积将最近 30 帧本体感知观测压成隐变量 z_t，MLP 结合 z_t 与当前观测输出关节目标；训练时的接触解码器只给编码器提供监督，其预测不进入策略。

figure.caption: {Policy Architecture}. A temporal convolution compresses the last $H=30$ proprioceptive observations $o_t$ (joint positions $q$ and velocities $ q$, gripper pose $x$ and twist $ x$, and the previous action $a_{t-1}$) into a latent $z_t$, and an MLP maps $z_t$ and the current observation $o_t$ to joint targets $q_d$ for a joint impedance controller. During training, we provide contact supervision from privileged simulator state. A contact decoder (amber) predicts the contact state ($ c_t$) from $z_t$. Its cross-entropy $ {L}_ {contact}$ with the simulator's labels $c_t$ (left, near half of the fixture cut away) trains the encoder, but $ c_t$ never reaches the policy.

page_papers.title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
page_papers.abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.

Abstract
How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present
\dspfont
DSP
:
Dexterity from supervised play
, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490
×
\times
less interaction data. These results demonstrate that
supervised play
can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.
I
Introduction
Humans, especially infants and children, develop dexterity from playing
[
1
]
. Play offers a task-agnostic source of interaction. Similarly, for robots, learning via playing holds tremendous potential for learning a rich physical understanding of the world required for dexterous manipulation without human supervision. In practice, however, play is a difficult behavior to engineer.
Fig. 1:
\dspfont
DSP
Pipeline Overview.
(1) Human teleoperation trains a goal-agnostic play policy. (2) The policy collects interaction data through autonomous play. (3) These data train a world model to predict future states from past observations and proposed actions. (4) MPC uses the model to select actions for a requested goal. (5) Optionally, we can distill a goal-conditioned policy from self-play in the learned world model.
Prior works model
play
by manually defining explicit heuristics as guidance
[
2
,
3
,
4
]
and by engineering restrictive safety boundaries to prevent hardware damage
[
5
]
. However, play is inherently intuitive and difficult to formalize with hand-crafted rules, while manual safety constraints require excessive tuning that limits scalability.
In this work, our core hypothesis is that play is a behavior that can be modeled as a ‘goal-agnostic’ state-conditioned probabilistic model in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and therefore be learned through a standard behavior cloning pipeline. In other words, even though a safe play behavior is hard to be defined explicitly with heuristics, it can easily be learned implicitly through demonstration data.
Fig. 2:
Dexterity from Supervised Play.
(a) A goal-agnostic play policy is trained by behavior cloning on human teleoperation data. (b) The learned policy interacts autonomously with the environment to collect observation–action transitions. (c) These transitions train an action-conditioned world model to predict future observations. (d) At inference time, the play policy proposes candidate actions, the world model predicts their outcomes, and model-predictive control selects the candidate with the highest goal-conditioned reward. The selected action is executed in the environment, and planning repeats from the new observation.
Therefore, we propose
\dspfont
DSP
:
Dexterity from Supervised Play
, a
framework that turns minutes of human play into a policy that can continue
collecting robot interaction autonomously. An action-conditioned world model
learns from these data, while the same play policy provides candidate action
sequences for model-predictive control (MPC). As a preliminary acceleration
study, we also explore distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy
through self-play within the learned world model.
Our primary contribution is a framework for learning dexterous manipulation
from data collected by an autonomous play policy. We evaluate how autonomous
play supports world-model learning and goal-directed planning through four
technical contributions:
•
Supervised play.
We formulate supervised play as a mechanism for turning a limited
human interaction prior into autonomous contact-rich data collection.
•
Scaling autonomous play data.
We show that held-out
world-model prediction improves monotonically as the real-robot
autonomous-play dataset grows from 0.5 to 5 hours.
•
Play policy as an action prior.
We show that using play policy as an action-proposal model for MPC significantly improves manipulation performance.
•
Self-play policy distillation
. A method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through world-model self-play to accelerate inference.
Experimental results show
\dspfont
DSP
reaches
within
0.6
0.6
rad on 91.4% of trials and within
0.4
0.4
rad on 72.7%, compared
with 53.9% and 25.8% for hindsight BC. PPO reaches 86.7% at both
thresholds after 344M counted frames, about 490 times the counted-frame
budget. Real world experiment shows
\dspfont
DSP
is able to transfer to real world with matched performance.
We further validate
\dspfont
DSP
on Push-T and visual in-hand manipulation, demonstrating that the framework generalizes across tasks and observation representations.
We also provide detailed analysis to carefully examine the characteristics of the proposed algorithm and the impacts of the
key design decisions. The code, data, and training details will
be publicly available for reproducing our results.
II
Related Work
II-A
Play and interaction in RL
RL agents can acquire sophisticated behavior via open-ended interaction and planning. Model-based
agents such as MuZero
[
6
]
learn a latent dynamics model and plan within it to master
board games and Atari without access to the rules.
In multi-agent settings, emergent autocurricula produce complex strategies purely from self-play and environment interaction, as in the
hide-and-seek tool-use environment
[
7
]
. Comparable
interaction-driven pipelines now reach elite performance on physical systems such
as competitive table tennis
[
5
]
. These results establish that
interaction and planning are powerful, but they depend on well-specified rewards,
simulators, or game rules.
\dspfont
DSP
instead targets contact-rich manipulation, where
reward engineering and designing safe exploration plans are difficult, and obtains its
behavior from human play rather than from reward-driven search.
II-B
Curiosity and intrinsic motivation
To reduce dependence on hand-designed rewards, intrinsic-motivation methods reward
the agent for reaching novel or hard-to-predict states.
Prediction-error curiosity uses the error of a learned forward as an intrinsic signal
[
3
,
8
]
, while Random Network Distillation measures novelty as the error of predicting a fixed random network’s features
[
9
]
. While such signals drive broad exploration, they are still heuristics and they do not bias interactions toward safe, object-centric contact that dexterous manipulation requires.
II-C
Learning from play
Closest to our framing is robot learning from play: goal-free, human-generated
interaction used as a task-agnostic source of supervision. Play-LMP learns latent
plans from teleoperated play and reuses them for goal-conditioned control
[
10
]
, and subsequent work distills affordances from play to
improve sample efficiency
[
4
]
. These approaches largely treat play as a fixed dataset for imitation. In contrast,
\dspfont
DSP
uses a human play data seed to train a policy that serves as a reusable, autonomous data-collection mechanism.
II-D
Dexterous manipulation
Dexterous, multi-fingered manipulation has been approached both by model-free
reinforcement learning and by imitation. RL methods learn agile in-hand skills such
as general object reorientation
[
11
,
12
,
13
,
14
]
and
sim-to-real cube manipulation
[
15
,
16
,
17
]
, but require carefully shaped task rewards and hundreds of millions of simulated
interactions.
\dspfont
DSP
differs from existing work and does not use simulation data: it learns contact-rich dynamics purely from autonomous play, without task-specific demonstrations or rewards, and plans for arbitrary goals by scoring
play-policy proposals with the learned world model under MPC.
III
Method
Fig. 3:
Dexterous skills emerge through play-guided planning.
MPC selects motions from a goal-agnostic play policy using their predicted outcomes, producing yaw rotations, edge and corner flips, fine adjustments, and composite actions without task-specific skill demonstrations. These examples illustrate how a shared repertoire of play motions can support both large reorientations and precise corrections toward a goal. Time progresses downward in each column; yellow arrows indicate object motion.
III-A
Overview
Given a dexterous manipulation task, our pipeline
\dspfont
DSP
achieves it in 4 stages described in Fig.
2
. We first collect data through teleoperation to train a play policy (see Sec.
III-B
). We then rollout this policy on the robot autonomously to collect a play dataset that contains observation–action transitions (see Sec.
III-C

III-D

III-E

Analysis
Inference time in Real-world.
Table
IV
summarizes real-world inference latency. Perception and planning run on a single RTX 5090 over a local network. Cube tracking keeps pace with the 30fps camera, while each replan takes 134ms: 61ms for sampling 1024 play-policy proposals, 44ms for batched world-model rollout, and 23ms for scoring and refinement. Real-time control is enabled by batched candidate evaluation and action chunking: planning overlaps execution of the current action prefix, so the hand continues moving while the next plan is computed. This allows the closed-loop system to operate in real time at 15–18Hz.

V
Discussion
V-A
\dspfont
DSP
vs. behavior cloning
Supervised play changes the role of human demonstrations: rather than specifying how to solve each task, they specify how to sustain useful interaction with the environment. Goal-agnostic behavior is not unstructured behavior. Choices about maintaining contact, safe exploration, and transitioning between grasps contain physical knowledge even without a prescribed outcome. Learning this interaction priors allows human guidance to support experience beyond the demonstrations themselves. In this view, the primary purpose of supervision is not a finished controller or a dataset of expert demonstrations, but a mechanism for collecting further data. This offers a more efficient approach to leveraging human supervision: humans provide the behavioral structure needed to begin interacting, while the robot acquires knowledge of action consequences through its own experience.
Additionally, demonstrating play behavior is almost always easier than demonstrating solution to a dexterous manipulation task. And in this paper, we show that a goal-agnostic policy is learnable via human demonstration and is highly data-efficient.
V-B
\dspfont
DSP
vs. RL
Compared to task-specific RL which organizes learning around reward optimization,
\dspfont
DSP
separates acquiring physical knowledge from task goal. The goal enters at planning time, allowing the same interaction prior and world model to serve different target goals without retraining. Learning dynamics directly from autonomous robot interaction also removes the prerequisite of a task-specific simulator and subsequent sim-to-real transfer. Supervised play is therefore not merely an initialization for RL, but the basis of a complete learning-and-control framework. It opens a route to scaling dexterity through reusable physical experience, with human guidance initiating autonomous learning rather than prescribing the behaviors it must ultimately achieve.
V-C
\dspfont
DSP
vs. curiosity vs. random exploration
Curiosity-driven exploration typically rewards novelty or prediction error, but these objectives do not, by themselves, specify the sustained, coordinated object interaction needed for dexterous manipulation, which has been a pain point in applying curiosity in contact-rich manipulation. Our approach addresses this challenge by learning the structure of interaction from human play, rather than requiring it to emerge through intrinsic-reward, which is especially important for contact-rich manipulation tasks. This suggests a broader principle for embodied learning: useful exploration need not be discovered from scratch through a generic novelty objective. Human intuition can supply its behavioral structure, while autonomous interaction supplies the physical knowledge needed to turn that structure into dexterity.
V-D
Behavior foundation models as play policies.
The modular role of the play policy suggests a possible connection to behavior foundation models
[
21
]
. A broader pretrained model could provide an initial repertoire of interactions, while autonomous experience grounds their predicted consequences in a particular robot and environment. A promising future direction is to leverage large behavior models and turn them into a generalizable play policy.

VI
Conclusion
Dexterity from Supervised Play turns limited goal-free human play into
autonomous contact-rich data, an action-conditioned world model, and
goal-directed control through play-guided MPC. In simulation, the learned
model supports arbitrary-goal reorientation with far fewer interactions than
PPO-Match in counted training frames, and a
controlled model-stack comparison shows improved goal acquisition under a
fixed planner. On real-robot data,
held-out prediction improves monotonically as autonomous play grows. A
provisional hardware summary is consistent with a benefit from world-model
search, but requires a frozen protocol and uncertainty before supporting a
final task-success claim. The final evaluation includes both Push-T and RGB
reorientation; their frozen quantitative results, together with curiosity and
matched play-policy and world-model architecture comparisons, remain to be
inserted.

article.headline: 人类玩耍几分钟，机器人自主采数据学灵巧操作
article.lede: 机器人先用几分钟人类遥操作学会「无目标玩耍」，再自主玩几小时采集数据训练世界模型，由 MPC 完成任意目标的手内重定向。
article.problem: 接触丰富的灵巧操作需要大量交互数据，但在真实硬件上做任务奖励工程和安全探索代价很高。已有工作把「玩耍」写成显式启发式规则或手工安全边界，前者难以形式化，后者需要大量调参、难以扩展。此前的「从玩耍学习」也大多只把玩耍轨迹当作固定的模仿数据集，无法让机器人自己继续采集数据。
article.method: 作者提出 DSP：先用行为克隆在几分钟无目标的人类遥操作数据上训练一个 goal-agnostic 的 diffusion-transformer 玩耍策略，再把它部署到机器人上自主 rollout，采集 observation–action–next observation 转移。随后用 Diffusion Forcing 在这些数据上训练动作条件世界模型，预测给定动作块后的未来观测。推理时由玩耍策略采样 1024 条候选动作块，世界模型预测其后果，MPC 按目标奖励挑出最优者并执行前若干步后重规划；此外还可在世界模型内自博弈、蒸馏出闭环的 goal-conditioned 策略以摊销推理开销。
article.results: 在仿真手内重定向（初始与目标姿态相差超过 90°）中，DSP 在 0.6 rad 阈值下成功率 91.4%、0.4 rad 下 72.7%，hindsight BC 分别为 53.9% 和 25.8%；PPO 在两个阈值上都是 86.7%，但需要 344M 帧，约为 DSP 的 490 倍交互数据。真实机器人上用 Sharpa 手把立方体转到任意目标姿态，DSP 达到 68.6/90.0/97.1%（0.4/0.6/0.8 rad），论文称成功率比 hindsight BC 高 69.6%，与仿真的 72.7/91.4/96.1% 在每个阈值上相差不超过 4.1 个百分点。Push-T 上 DSP 为 98%/74%（SR@0.90、SR@0.95），hindsight BC 为 74%/36%，覆盖率从 0.764 升到 0.953；同数据预算下的 PPO 为 0%/0%。真实机器人自主玩耍数据从 0.54 小时增至 5.11 小时，50 步旋转 MAE 从 34.96° 单调降到 28.40°（降 18.8%，比 persistence 基线 38.60° 低 26.4%）。蒸馏策略在 0.4/0.6/0.8 rad 上为 40.6/72.7/86.7%，单次推理 21.8 ms，比一次 MPC 重规划快 7 倍；MPC 端到端重规划中位延迟 133.6 ms，系统以 15–18Hz 闭环运行。
article.why_it_matters: 它把人类监督的角色从「演示每个任务怎么解」换成「给一个能持续自主采数据的交互先验」，学到的玩耍策略和世界模型不绑定具体目标，换目标只需换奖励，也不需要任务专用仿真器或 sim-to-real 迁移。相比依赖内在好奇心奖励的探索，它用人类玩耍直接提供了接触丰富操作所需的行为结构。
article.limitations: 论文自身承认，真实硬件结果只是「provisional」的初步汇总，还需在冻结协议和误差评估下才能支撑最终的任务成功率结论，且 Push-T 与 RGB 重定向的冻结定量结果、与 curiosity 及匹配架构的对照「仍待插入」；视觉重定向只有 64 次试验、3600 步时域，作者明言只用于验证表征迁移而非协议匹配的对比，正文与 Table II 对 RGB 结果的标注也不一致（表中把 56.2/78.1/89.1% 标为 state-space）。此外方法仍需人类遥操作用作种子数据，玩耍数据的边际收益在约两小时后明显变缓，实测仅覆盖到 5 小时量级，MPC 单次重规划 134 ms 也依赖动作分块、并行候选评估和 15–18Hz 的降频控制。
article.figure_caption_zh: DSP 流程：人类遥操作训练无目标玩耍策略→策略自主玩耍采集交互数据→训练动作条件世界模型→MPC 依据目标挑选动作→可选地在世界模型内自博弈蒸馏闭环策略。

figure.caption: { Pipeline Overview.} (1) Human teleoperation trains a goal-agnostic play policy. (2) The policy collects interaction data through autonomous play. (3) These data train a world model to predict future states from past observations and proposed actions. (4) MPC uses the model to select actions for a requested goal. (5) Optionally, we can distill a goal-conditioned policy from self-play in the learned world model.

page_papers.title: RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
page_papers.abstract: Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data. Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation. In this work, we propose RoboFFT, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates. We evaluate RoboFFT with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that RoboFFT consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate RoboFFT into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website: https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/.
page_papers.content:
RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
Yu Li
Shenghe Hu
Yuhan Wang
Yaoxiang Pu
Haotong Zhang
Yuanpei Chen
Yaodong Yang
Abstract
Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data.
Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation.
In this work, we propose
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that
RoboFFT
consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate
RoboFFT
into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website:
https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/
.
Figure 1:
We present
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policy with forward process. (a) Reverse finetuning formulates the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP, while forward finetuning aligns with the same objective as training by following the forward noising process.
(b) One framework across popular generative robot policy on simulation benchmarks.
(c) Real-world deployment with integration of real world RL.
(d) Improved performance in success rate, training stability and efficiency.

Keywords:
Diffusion RL, Generative Robot Policy, Robot Manipulation
1
Introduction
Generative robot policies, typically based on diffusion and flow-based models
[
43
,
42
,
15
,
29
]
, have become a powerful paradigm for learning visuomotor skills from demonstrations by modeling complex and multi-modal action distributions
[
12
,
56
,
53
]
, which significantly improves robot action accuracy and robustness and yields substantial performance gains in complex manipulation tasks
[
12
,
53
]
. However, policies trained purely by imitation learning remain constrained by the quality and coverage of the demonstration data. Imperfect demonstrations, covariate shift, and insufficient exposure to deployment-time states can all limit the final task performance of behavior-cloned policies
[
13
,
40
]
. Online reinforcement learning (RL) naturally presents itself as a promising paradigm to further improve generative robot policies, as it empowers the policy to directly maximize task rewards by continuously interacting with and learning from the environment.
Applying policy gradient RL methods to generative robot policies is nevertheless nontrivial. Unlike autoregressive policies, whose token likelihoods are tractable, diffusion and flow-based models typically lack a tractable exact likelihood formulation. This makes popular policy gradient objectives, such as PPO, difficult to be applied directly. Existing approaches address this issue by formulating the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP embedded in the high-level environment MDP, and optimizing through this two-level decision making trajectory
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
(Fig.
1
(a), left). Despite its promising results, reverse-process finetuning introduces substantial computation and memory overhead, and may suffer from gradient instability due to long denoising chains, especially in high-dimensional and long-horizon manipulation tasks.
To address these issues, we propose
RoboFFT
, a simpler yet more effective framework for online RL finetuning of generative robot manipulation policies through the
forward
noising process, inspired by recent studies from other application domains such as image generation and simple locomotion
[
52
,
59
,
34
]
. Instead of assigning credit through the reverse denoising chain,
RoboFFT
approximates the exact log-likelihood with a more computationally stable and efficient form akin to the score / flow matching loss for pretraining, yielding a principled PPO-style objective that is aligned with the imitation-learning objective while avoiding complicated likelihood computation or backpropagation through the full reverse trajectory. For flow-based policies, we further adopt SDE sampling by injecting noise into the sampling process, enabling controllable exploration during online data collection. In practice, Monte Carlo estimation, ratio-temperature calibration and further adaptations make likelihood estimation and updates robust across different policy architectures and tasks.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
on challenging robot manipulation benchmarks such as Robomimic
[
33
]
and LIBERO
[
30
]
, which pose difficulties like high-dimensional visual observation, long horizon planning and sparse reward for finetuning. Experimental results across different tasks demonstrate substantial and consistent performance improvements over pretrained diffusion and flow policies and achieve competitive or better performance compared with representative reverse and forward process finetuning baselines, while reducing optimization overhead. We further verify the applicability of our method on more complicated VLA and real world deployment settings, and study the key designs through ablations and visualizations. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) We introduce
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework that performs policy gradient finetuning in the forward noising process for generative robot policies.
(2) We carry out practical implementation of
RoboFFT
for representative generative robot policies (flow, diffusion and VLA) on challenging long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks, showing that
RoboFFT
achieves superior performance and improved training stability and efficiency.
(3) We integrate
RoboFFT
into the real world reinforcement learning framework for practical deployment and demonstrate its effectiveness over real world tasks.
(4) We carry out a systematic ablation analysis of key design choices and conduct investigative experiments to provide empirical insights for the mechanism of
RoboFFT
.
2
Related Work
2.1
Policy Gradient for Robot Manipulation
Policy gradient and actor critic methods provide a standard framework for learning continuous-control policies from interaction data
[
50
,
45
,
28
,
41
]
. Due to the
training stability with high-dimensional action spaces, they have been widely applied to a range of robotic control problems, including dexterous manipulation, legged locomotion, and agile navigation
[
48
,
9
,
10
,
1
,
17
,
21
]
. For long-horizon manipulation, however, training from scratch remains highly exploration-intensive and is often impractical. A more practical paradigm is therefore to finetune policies initialized from demonstration data. Prior studies have shown that reinforcement learning can further improve such demonstration-initialized policies beyond behavior cloning while substantially reducing the exploration burden
[
38
,
46
,
37
]
. RoboFFT follows this finetuning paradigm, while focusing on diffusion- and flow-based robot policies whose action distributions are implicitly induced by generative sampling processes, making the likelihood ratio computation required by policy gradient methods nontrivial.
2.2
RL for Generative Models
Reinforcement learning has recently been widely applied to generative model finetuning in offline
[
3
,
35
,
16
,
49
,
14
,
36
,
7
]
, offline-to-online
[
11
,
26
]
, and online settings
[
39
,
57
,
54
,
34
,
52
,
59
]
. Online finetuning for diffusion and flow models can be broadly categorized into reverse-process and forward-process approaches. Reverse-process methods formulate the denoising or sampling trajectory as a multi-step decision process, enabling tractable per-step likelihood for policy optimization
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
. While effective, optimizing through long internal sampling chains can increase computation and memory costs and may introduce training instability. Forward-process methods instead optimize policy via constructing surrogate likelihood objectives or contrastive learning, better aligning RL finetuning with generative pretraining
[
52
,
34
,
54
,
59
]
. DiffusionNFT and AWM
[
59
,
52
]
study this idea for text-to-image generation. FPO and FPO++
[
34
,
54
]
extend it to robotic control, but mainly focus on locomotion tasks. In comparison, RoboFFT studies forward-process finetuning in more challenging robotic manipulation, and covers more extensive settings including both diffusion and flow policies, VLA finetuning, and real world deployment with practical stabilization designs.

Evaluation on Real World
To evaluate the effectiveness of
RoboFFT
on real world robotic manipulation tasks, we integrate our method into a practical real-world RL framework
[

[
26

RoboFFT
to an offline-to-online formulation while retaining its core components including forward noising, the matching loss surrogate ratio, and PPO-style clipping. Specifically, we first pretrain a flow-based policy using human demonstrations collected via SpaceMouse teleoperation.
We then perform multiple offline RL iterations. In each offline iteration, we perform offline PPO-style optimization on the collected rollout data, where IQL
[
25
]
is used to estimate advantages from offline trajectories. After each offline RL update, we deploy the updated policy on the real robot to collect additional trajectories, which are added to the offline dataset for the next offline RL iteration. To stabilize policy improvement and avoid drifting away from reliable human behaviors, we combine the newly collected rollout data with the original teleoperation demonstrations and conduct imitation learning to update the base policy for the next iteration.

6
Limitations
Although
RoboFFT
enables stable online finetuning of generative robot policies through the forward noising process, it still has several limitations. First, the weighted score/flow matching loss is only a surrogate for the true action log-likelihood, and its scale may vary across noise schedules, action dimensions, and policy architectures. Therefore, additional calibration such as temperature scaling is still needed to ensure stable PPO-style updates. Second, our current framework relies on on-policy PPO, which has limited data efficiency and cannot fully reuse historical trajectories. This makes real-world deployment challenging, especially when data collection is restricted to a single robot. Although offline-to-online paradigms such as RL100
[
26
]
can partially alleviate this issue, they usually require iterative data collection and offline retraining, which remains time-consuming in practice. Future work may explore more sample-efficient variants that better leverage historical trajectories and human intervention data for safer and faster real world robot learning.
7
Conclusion
We present
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies. By applying forward noising to sampled actions and using the weighted score/flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio,
RoboFFT
enables PPO-style policy optimization without requiring explicit likelihood estimation. Experiments on representative simulation benchmarks show that
RoboFFT
consistently improves popular generative robot policies on long-horizon and sparse-reward manipulation tasks, while achieving better training stability and efficiency. Further integration into a real world RL framework also demonstrates its effectiveness on real robot tasks.

B.1
Robomimic Benchmark
We use Robomimic
[
33
]
as the simulated manipulation benchmark throughout our main experiments. Robomimic provides sparse-reward robot manipulation tasks collected from human demonstrations, making it a suitable testbed for evaluating whether online finetuning can improve a behavior-cloned generative policy beyond its initial demonstration-trained performance. Following the data processing and environment conventions used in DPPO and ReinFlow
[
39
,
57
]
, we evaluate four Robomimic tasks: Lift, Can, Square, and Transport. The corresponding observation and action specifications are summarized in Table
1
.
The four tasks cover different manipulation difficulties. Lift requires the robot to grasp and lift an object, while Can is a pick-and-place task where the robot must manipulate a can into the target container. Square is a more precision-sensitive assembly task in which the robot must manipulate a square nut and place it onto a positioning peg. Transport is a long-horizon bimanual manipulation task that requires coordinated control of two robot arms to move an object across the workspace. Thus, the benchmark spans both short-horizon single-arm manipulation and longer-horizon bimanual manipulation.
We consider both state-input and pixel-input variants. In the state-input setting, the policy observes low-dimensional proprioceptive and object state features. In the pixel-input setting, the policy observes RGB image(s) at
96
×
96
96\times 96

B.4
Baseline Methods and Configurations
We compare RoboFFT with representative online RL fine-tuning baselines for diffusion- and flow-based robot policies.
DPPO.
Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization
[
39
]
is a representative reverse-process fine-tuning method for diffusion policies. It formulates the reverse denoising process together with the environment interaction process as a two-level MDP, and applies PPO to optimize the Gaussian likelihoods of denoising transitions. We use DPPO as the canonical diffusion-policy RL baseline for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
ReinFlow.
ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends the reverse-process policy-gradient paradigm to flow-based policies. It injects stochasticity into the deterministic flow trajectory, turns the sampler into a discrete-time Markov process with tractable Gaussian transition probabilities, and performs PPO-style optimization over the internal sampling trajectory. We use ReinFlow as the primary flow-policy baseline.
FPO.
Flow Policy Optimization
[
34
]
is a forward-process policy-gradient method that constructs a PPO-style surrogate ratio from conditional flow matching losses. We adapt FPO into our online fine-tuning codebase for Robomimic. To ensure fair comparison under the same tasks and pretrained policies, most environment and optimizer settings are shared with RoboFFT. The main algorithmic differences are that FPO does not use our SDE explorative sampling strategy and ratio-temperature calibration adopted in RoboFFT, while following the original FPO convention of using

DRWR.
DRWR is a lightweight diffusion reward-weighted regression baseline following the implementation convention in DPPO
[
39
]
. It performs forward-noise matching style updates weighted by rewards or returns, and serves as a simple forward-process reference that is architecturally close to our approach but does not use the PPO-style objective and the many critical designs introduced by our work.
For all baselines, we match the Robomimic environment wrappers, observation preprocessing, action chunking, base-policy training data, and evaluation protocol whenever applicable. The hyperparameters of DPPO, ReinFlow, and DRWR follow their original implementations unless a task-specific adaptation is necessary. Since the released ReinFlow manipulation implementation focuses on pixel-input Robomimic tasks, for state-input tasks we adapt secondary settings such as optimizer and update-batch configurations while keeping the core ReinFlow design unchanged. For fair comparison, the number of inference steps and finetuning steps are tuned on each task, so that each baseline achieves its nearly best performance. RoboFFT-F and RoboFFT-D are respectively implemented upon the ReinFlow

and DPPO

Additional Analyses for the Robomimic Experiments
C.1
Performance Analysis
This subsection provides additional discussion for the main Robomimic comparison in Sec.
5.1
, where the comprehensive performance of RoboFFT-F, RoboFFT-D and the baseline methods are evaluated under both state-input and pixel-input settings.
Across the easier
Lift
and
Can
tasks, RoboFFT-D and RoboFFT-F reach final success rates comparable to reverse-process baselines such as DPPO and ReinFlow. Their convergence can be slightly slower in some early-stage curves, but the final policy quality remains competitive. This suggests that the forward-process surrogate ratio preserves enough policy-gradient signal for improving already competent pretrained policies, while avoiding explicit likelihood computation through the reverse denoising chain.
The advantage of RoboFFT becomes more pronounced on the harder tasks. On
Square
and
Transport
, especially with pixel observations, RoboFFT shows a more sustained improvement trend and stronger final performance. Reverse-process methods can suffer from instability or later performance recession, likely because optimizing through a long internal sampling chain introduces a more complicated credit-assignment path and a heavier computation graph, making the gradients and parameter updates instable. In comparison, RoboFFT directly applies forward noising to the final rollout action and optimizes a matching-loss-based surrogate ratio, which keeps the optimization path closer to imitation pretraining.
The forward-process baselines, DRWR and FPO, are generally less competitive in the Robomimic manipulation setting. DRWR uses reward-weighted regression and does not include a PPO-style trust region, making it more sensitive to high-variance reward weights in sparse-reward tasks. FPO uses a forward-process PPO-style ratio, but in our implementation it lacks the manipulation-oriented stabilization designs used in RoboFFT, including controlled SDE exploration and ratio-temperature calibration. These differences help explain why simply applying a forward matching loss is not sufficient for robust online fine-tuning on long-horizon manipulation tasks.

Compared with the pretrained policy, whose sampled action chunks are more diffusely distributed and contain many low- or negative-advantage samples, the finetuned policy forms a more concentrated region with noticeably higher diagnostic advantages. Appendix H
Extended Related Work
H.1
Generative Models for Robot Manipulation
Generative models have become an increasingly important policy class for robot manipulation, as they provide expressive distributions over complex and potentially multimodal action sequences. Early approaches
[
58
,
27
]
formulate imitation learning with a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). More recently, diffusion-based policies have demonstrated substantially greater expressiveness for continuous control. Diffusion Policy
[
12
,
19
]
models the conditional action distribution through an iterative denoising process, enabling stable learning of high-dimensional and multimodal action distributions and motivating a broad family of diffusion-based manipulation policies. Flow-matching models provide an alternative generative formulation by learning continuous transport from a simple noise distribution to the action distribution. Methods such as ManiFlow
[
53
]
further improve sampling efficiency and policy expressiveness through consistency-based flow training, demonstrating strong performance on diverse manipulation tasks. In parallel, vision-language-action (VLA) models have extended robot policies toward large-scale generalist control by leveraging pretrained vision-language representations and heterogeneous robot datasets. RT-2
[
6
]
and OpenVLA
[
22
]
generate discretized robot actions within large autoregressive vision-language models, while
π
0
\pi_{0}
[
4
]
and
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
[
18
]
combine a pretrained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert for continuous action generation.
H.2
RL for Generative Robot Policy
Reinforcement learning has been increasingly explored to improve generative policies beyond behavior cloning. Early studies mainly focus on offline RL with fixed datasets. Diffusion Q Learning
[
49
]
parameterizes the actor as a diffusion model and combines diffusion regression with Q value maximization, while IDQL
[
14
]
uses an implicit Q-function to select actions sampled from a diffusion behavior policy. This idea has also been extended to flow-based policies. Flow Q Learning (FQL)
[
36
]
learns a flow matching behavior policy together with a one-step RL policy, avoiding recursive differentiation through iterative flow generation. Although these methods exploit the expressiveness of generative policies, their improvement is constrained by the coverage of the offline dataset and the accuracy of learned value functions.
More recent work considers online or offline-to-online adaptation of pretrained generative robot policies. One direction keeps the base policy frozen and learns a lightweight steering or residual component. DSRL
[
47
]
performs RL in the latent-noise space of a pretrained diffusion or flow policy without modifying its parameters, while residual RL methods learn corrective actions on top of a frozen behavior cloning policy
[
2
,
44
,
20
]
. These approaches preserve pretrained behaviors and reduce the complexity of online optimization, but restrict policy improvement to the residual or latent space exposed by the frozen policy.
In contrast, full policy finetuning directly updates the generative model parameters. DPPO
[
39
]
formulates diffusion denoising as a multi-step MDP and applies PPO over reverse denoising transitions. ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends likelihood-based online optimization to flow policies by injecting stochasticity into deterministic flow trajectories. Forward process methods such as FPO
[
34
]
and its extensions
[
54
]
instead construct policy-gradient objectives from flow matching losses, avoiding explicit marginal likelihood computation. Reinforced finetuning has also been extended to VLA policies, with
[
11
,
51
]
combining offline value learning and online policy optimization for real-world manipulation. RoboFFT belongs to the full policy finetuning family, but performs PPO-style optimization through the forward noising process, providing a unified framework for diffusion, flow, and VLA policies.

article.headline: RoboFFT：前向加噪微调机器人策略
article.lede: 北大等单位提出RoboFFT，用前向加噪匹配损失构造PPO替代比率，在线微调扩散、流匹配与VLA机器人策略。
article.problem: 扩散和流匹配机器人策略能从演示中学习多模态动作，但纯模仿学习受演示质量、协变量偏移和部署状态覆盖不足限制。在线强化学习可直接用任务奖励改进策略，但这类生成式策略没有可 tractable 的精确似然，PPO式更新难以直接应用。现有反向去噪链微调计算和显存开销大，长链还可能带来梯度不稳定。
article.method: RoboFFT先用遥操作数据以score/flow matching损失预训练生成式策略，在线阶段用SDE采样器收集动作并接收环境奖励。对每个采样动作做前向加噪，复用加权score/flow matching损失作为替代负对数似然，构造新旧策略的替代比率，并进行PPO式裁剪更新。实现上采用蒙特卡洛估计和比率温度校准，避免对完整反向采样链求似然或反传。
article.results: 在Robomimic上，RoboFFT-F对ReinFlow取得平均1.53×训练时间加速，RoboFFT-D在四个状态输入任务上对DPPO平均加速38.0×，且仍使用N_mc=16。真实任务Pick Eggplant成功率从预训练12/20、离线18/20提升到在线20/20；同数据预算下BC Agg.为14/20、DRWR为12/20，在线RoboFFT达到20/20并与RL100持平。其他真实任务中，Peg Insertion从10/20到20/20，Pour从9/20到18/20，Cabinet Retrieval从5/20到17/20；LIBERO-VLA实验正文未给出具体成功率数字，仅以图5曲线展示。
article.why_it_matters: 它把生成式策略的RL后训练拉回到与预训练一致的匹配损失上，为扩散、流匹配和VLA策略提供统一的在线微调路径。真实机器人实验显示，任务级交互反馈可进一步提升预训练策略，而不必只依赖更多专家演示。
article.limitations: 作者指出，匹配损失只是真实动作对数似然的替代，其尺度会随噪声日程、动作维度和策略架构变化，仍需温度缩放等校准；Square-state诊断中替代比率与参考的Spearman秩相关仅约0.2。框架依赖on-policy PPO，数据效率有限、难以充分复用历史轨迹，真实部署还需迭代采集和离线重训，耗时较长。
article.figure_caption_zh: RoboFFT流程：先用遥操作数据预训练生成式策略，在线用SDE采样收集动作并由环境给奖励，再对动作前向加噪，以匹配损失构造替代似然进行PPO式更新。

figure.caption: Overview of {RoboFFT}. We first collect the offline data leveraging teleoperation and pretrain the base policy with the score / flow matching loss. The pretrained policy then generates actions using an SDE sampler and receives reward feedback from the environment. Finally, we apply forward noising and reuse the matching loss as a surrogate likelihood for PPO-style policy update.

journals.title: Towards understanding and monitorability of reasoning LLMs
journals.summary:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01333-6

Frontier LLMs are trained to solve problems in a step-by-step way, generating reasoning text in human-understandable language. However, these reasoning tokens are not accurate explanations of LLMs’ internal computations, raising challenges for monitorability.
journals.blurb: 《Nature Machine Intelligence》刊文讨论推理型大语言模型的可理解性与可监控性。前沿模型会以人类可读语言逐步生成推理文本，但这些推理 token 并不构成对模型内部计算的准确解释，从而给监控带来挑战。

journals.title: Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03313-7

Large language models can mimic thought and feeling with uncanny skill. But evidence from neuroscience suggests that intelligence alone is not enough for subjective experience.
journals.blurb: Nature 刊文讨论大语言模型为何不被视为具有意识：它们能逼真模仿思考与情感，但神经科学证据表明，仅有智能不足以产生主观体验。对机器学习研究生而言，这提示在评估模型能力时需区分行为表现与内在体验，不宜将拟人化输出等同于意识。
